Revisiting the (Sub)Optimality of Best-of-N for Inference-Time Alignment

Ved Sriraman ††thanks: ved@cs.columbia.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Columbia University    Adam Block ††thanks: adam.block@columbia.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Columbia University Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Columbia University
Abstract

Best-of-NN (BoN) sampling is a widely used inference-time alignment method for language models, whereby NN candidate responses are sampled from a reference model and the one with the highest predicted reward according to a learned reward model is selected. Despite its widespread practical use, recent theoretical work has suggested that it is statistically suboptimal and vulnerable to reward hacking, the process by which models exploit weaknesses in the learned reward model to achieve high estimated reward without genuinely improving performance. We revisit this question under assumptions that more closely reflect practice than that of prior work. In particular, in contradistinction to earlier analyses that focused on expected true reward, which may not be meaningful in many practical settings, we investigate how inference-time alignment affects the win-rate, a pairwise comparison-based metric more closely aligned with how reward models are trained and evaluated in practice. We demonstrate that, under minimal conditions on the quality of the reference model and learned reward model, properly tuned BoN is both computationally and statistically optimal in achieving high win-rate, partially explaining its widespread practical success. Because BoN remains susceptible to reward-hacking in this setting, we propose a simple and practical variant that provably eliminates reward-hacking while maintaining optimal statistical performance. Finally, we show that prior approaches are provably suboptimal when considering win-rate, highlighting the importance of choosing appropriate objectives when analyzing inference-time alignment methods.

1 Introduction

Inference-time compute has emerged as a critical new scaling axis in Language Models (LMs) over the past few years, resulting in major advances in mathematical reasoning, coding ability, and reliability [5, 12, 15]. Previous works have identified two primary approaches to scaling inference-time compute: (i) parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple outputs in parallel and selects the one to return to a user; and (ii) serial scaling, where a model generates a much longer output that allows it access to computationally more involved solutions [22]. While both approaches have demonstrated significant empirical success, parallel scaling is particularly appealing due to its simplicity, ease of implementation, and ability to leverage existing models without additional training, with a number of empirical results demonstrating strong performance improvements from parallel scaling alone [5, 11, 13]. Additionally, the current approach to training models using Reinforcement Learning to take advantage of serial scaling relies critically on parallel scaling in order to estimate reward signals during the training process [12]. Thus, understanding the theoretical underpinnings of parallel scaling is a critical step towards understanding the capabilities of modern LMs.

The critical question that arises in the parallel scaling regime is how best to select the final returned output from a set of NN independently sampled candidates. Initial empirical approaches focused on verifiable settings, where the model’s output could be directly scored against a known ground-truth reward r⋆​(x,y)r^{\star}(x,y) depending on a prompt xx and candidate response yy; in this setting, the highest-scoring candidate could be selected [5]. While such an approach leads to a strong skyline performance, it is not applicable in the vast majority of real-world settings where no such verification is possible. Instead, it has become the standard pracatice to use some learned proxy reward r^​(x,y)\widehat{r}(x,y), again depending on the prompt and candidate response, to select the best candidate [29, 30, 23, 33, 21]; such an approach leads to the well-known Best-of-N (BoN) algorithm that returns y^N∈argmaxyir^​(x,yi)\hat{y}_{N}\in\argmax_{y_{i}}\widehat{r}(x,y_{i}). While the BoN algorithm has demonstrated strong empirical performance across a variety of settings and has seen some prior theoretical work [13, 14], there remain critical lacunae in our understanding of its behavior.

In Huang et al. [14], the authors provide a theoretical analysis of the BoN algorithm in the setting where the learned reward r^\widehat{r} is close to the true reward r⋆r^{\star} in terms of mean-squared error under the sampling distribution πref(⋅|x)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x) used to generate candidates yiy_{i} and demonstrate reasonable performance compared to some ‘good’ language model π⋆\pi^{\star} as long as π⋆\pi^{\star} is close to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} in an appropriate sense. Critically, however, they demonstrate that the BoN algorithm is suboptimal in this setting and that in order to achieve optimal performance, one must instead use a more sophisticated (and complicated) χ2\chi^{2}-regularized variant of the BoN algorithm introduced therein. This suboptimality arises due to another drawback of BoN: when the number of candidates NN is large, the algorithm engages in reward-hacking, a manifestation of Goodhart’s law [10] whereby the algorithm selects candidates that achieve high reward r^\widehat{r} but are in fact low-quality according to the true reward r⋆r^{\star} [9]. The χ2\chi^{2}-regularized BoN algorithm is able to mitigate this reward-hacking behavior by penalizing candidates that are unlikely under the sampling distribution πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, leading to improved performance. While an attractive theoretical result, the empirical relevance of this suboptimality is unclear, as optimally tuned BoN algorithms mostly outperformed the more complicated χ2\chi^{2}-regularized variant in practice, either statistically (leading to better performance) or computationally (requiring fewer samples to achieve the same performance).

The gap between theory and practice in Huang et al. [14] is partially explained by the fact that the authors in that paper recognize that in the special case where rewards are binary, as is often the case in reasoning tasks where outputs are either correct or incorrect, the BoN algorithm is in fact optimal when the number of candidate responses NN is properly tuned.11 1 Technically, in that work the authors allow for comparator policies with uniformly bounded likelihood ratios, but such an assumption is unlikely to hold for reasonable π⋆\pi^{\star} in the absence of binary rewards due to the increasingly long generations from modern LMs. On the other hand, in many situations, such as open-ended generation tasks like dialog or creative writing, rewards are not binary but instead take on a wide range of values depending on the quality of the response. In such settings, it remains unclear whether the BoN algorithm is optimal or suboptimal, and if suboptimal, whether more complicated variants can outperform it in practice. Moreover, in any setting, it remains unclear whether the mean-squared error metric used in Huang et al. [14] is the most appropriate way to measure the quality of learned reward models r^\widehat{r} and what the appropriate notion of ‘closeness’ between the sampling distribution πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and the target language model π⋆\pi^{\star} should be. In addition, the performance metric studied in that work is the expected true reward, which is often not very meaningful in many practical situations, where win-rate with respect to some comparator policy (cf. (2)) is a more natural evaluation [20].

In this work, we aim to address these open questions by providing a more complete theoretical understanding of the BoN algorithm that we believe better fits the empirical realities in which it is used, as well as present a new algorithm that is both theoretically optimal and provably mitigates reward-hacking. Our starting point is to observe that neither the mean-squared error metric for reward models nor the metric of expected true reward under the target language model are fully appropriate for understanding the performance of the BoN algorithm. Indeed, in most situations where rewards for language models are nonbinary, the ‘ground truth’ notion of reward is the win-rate, i.e., the proportion of times that some oracular alignment source (either human labellers or a strong LM) prefers the returned response to an offline reference response [20, 8, 7, 24]. Moreover, most reward models are trained in a similar manner, via pairwise comparisons between candidate responses rather than direct regression against some ground-truth reward value, which is rarely available in practice [27]. Indeed, there is a philosophical question to be asked as to the sense in which a ground-truth reward r⋆r^{\star} even exists when there is never direct supervision thereof; most empirical work asserts the Bradley-Terry model [4, 24] for practical purposes, but the expected reward remains a somewhat artificial construct.

Furthermore, while natural in the context of learning theory, the use of squared error is somewhat contrived in the context of the BoN algorithm in that it, unlike the algorithm itself, is not scale-invariant: multiplying the reward model r^\widehat{r} by a positive constant does not change the behavior of the BoN algorithm, but it does change the mean-squared error. Instead, a more natural notion of reward mismatch respects the way in which r^\widehat{r} is used in BoN, i.e., monotone transformations should not affect our quality metric. Finally, we address the ad hoc nature of the χ2\chi^{2}-regularized BoN algorithm by considering a substantially more general notion of quality, that of ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence [26], which was extensively studied in Block and Polyanskiy [2] and intimately connected to the recently introduced notion of coverage [13, 6], which has been fruitfully applied to understand LMs in a variety of settings.22 2 Formally, coverage is defined as CovM(π⋆∥πref)=ℙy∼π⋆(d​π⋆d​πref(y)≥M)\mathrm{Cov}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi^{\star}}\left(\frac{d\pi^{\star}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)\geq M\right). It is easy to see that ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=CovM(π⋆∥πref)−M⋅ℙy∼πref(d​π⋆d​πref(y)≥M)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathrm{Cov}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})-M\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\frac{d\pi^{\star}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)\geq M\right) is bounded above by coverage.

We have two main results in this work, the first of which is as follows.

Theorem 1 (Informal Statement of Theorems 3 and 4).

If r^\widehat{r} is close to r⋆r^{\star} in terms of pairwise win-rate error (cf. (3)), then the BoN algorithm using r^\widehat{r} with tuned NN achieves optimal performance.

This result demonstrates that when using an appropriate notion of reward model error that is commonly used in practice, the BoN algorithm is in fact optimal, somewhat opposing the practical intuition that arises from Huang et al. [14]. Indeed, while not a formal contradiction to the difference in formal settings, our result suggests that the suboptimality identified in Huang et al. [14] is an artifact of the assumptions therein rather than a fundamental limitation of the BoN algorithm.

On the other hand, the fundamental insight that reward-hacking can occur when NN is large remains valid, and thus we further introduce a new ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized BoN algorithm that directly penalizes candidates that are unlikely under the sampling distribution πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} in terms of the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence. Our second main result is as follows:

Theorem 2 (Informal Statement of Theorem 5).

If r^\widehat{r} is close to r⋆r^{\star} in terms of pairwise win-rate error, then the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized BoN algorithm (cf. (10)) using r^\widehat{r} with appropriately tuned regularization is both optimal and achieves performance that provably does not decay with NN.

This result demonstrates that by using ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularization, we can mitigate reward-hacking. A key advantage of our proposed algorithm over prior approaches to combatting reward overoptimization is the simplicity of implementation, which does not require online estimation, extensive additional training, or significant computational overhead beyond that of the BoN algorithm itself [14, 17, 16]. Moreover, we show in Proposition 2 that the χ2\chi^{2}-regularized BoN algorithm of Huang et al. [14] can be arbitrarily worse than our ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized BoN algorithm in terms of win-rate regret, demonstrating the insufficiency of prior approaches in this setting.

We now proceed in Section 2 by introducing and motivating our formal setting as well as clarifying how it differs from that considered in prior work, before stating our results for the BoN algorithm in Section 3. We then introduce our coverage-regularized BoN algorithm in Section 4 before discussing some key proof techniques in Section 5. While in much of the paper we consider a simplified setting where the comparator policy defining win-rate is equal to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, we extend our results to apply to settings where the win-rate is defined with respect to an arbitrary comparator in Section 6. We conclude with a discussion of related work and future directions in Section 7.

2 Preliminaries and Problem Setup

In this section, we introduce our inference-time alignment framework and formally state the problems we consider. We first describe the computational model through which we interact with language and reward models, before discussing the appropriate notions of model quality.

2.1 Inference-time alignment framework

Our framework is inspired by that of Huang et al. [13], Huang et al. [14], although we consider different desiderata. Throughout, we let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} denote a space of possible responses and 𝒳\mathcal{X} denote a space of possible prompts or contexts. A language model is any map π:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) from prompts to distributions over responses; due to the connections with RL, we use the terms language model and policy interchangeably. For the purposes of analysis, we will suppose that there exists a true reward function r⋆:𝒳×𝒴→ℝr^{\star}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} that measures the quality of a response yy given a prompt xx; in practice, this reward function will be unknown and only accessible through some learned reward model r^:𝒳×𝒴→ℝ\widehat{r}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}. For the sake of simplicity, we will always assume that 0≤r⋆​(x,y),r^​(x,y)≤Rmax0\leq r^{\star}(x,y),\widehat{r}(x,y)\leq R_{\mathrm{max}} for some known Rmax>0R_{\mathrm{max}}>0. As in Huang et al. [14], we will consider a simplified setting where the prompt xx is fixed throughout, and thus we will suppress it from notation for clarity, i.e., we will write πref​(⋅)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot) instead of πref(⋅|x)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x) and similarly for r⋆r^{\star} and r^\widehat{r}. Note that there is no loss of generality in doing so, as we can take expectations over the marginal distribution of prompts at the end of our analysis if desired.

We suppose that the learner has access to the following computational model, motivated by the fact that empirical LM inference engines like vLLM [18] can quickly sample from large language models and evaluate reward models in parallel.

Definition 1 (Sample-and-Evaluate).

The learner has access to a reference model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} from which he can sample responses y∼πrefy\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} independently. In addition, for any sampled response yy, the learner can query the reward model r^\widehat{r} to obtain the reward value r^​(y)\widehat{r}(y). The efficiency of the learner is measured by the total number of samples, NN, drawn from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}.

The goal of the learner is to use this sample-and-evaluate access to produce a response y^\hat{y} that achieves high true reward r⋆​(y^)r^{\star}(\hat{y}) while using as few samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} as possible. In order to evaluate candidate policies π^\widehat{\pi} producing responses y^∼π^\hat{y}\sim\widehat{\pi}, it is natural to compare them to some comparator policy π⋆\pi^{\star} that achieves high true reward through regret. While Huang et al. [14] consider regret in terms of expected true reward, i.e., trying to minimize 𝔼y∼π⋆​[r⋆​(y)]−𝔼y∼π^​[r⋆​(y)]\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{\star}}[r^{\star}(y)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\widehat{\pi}}[r^{\star}(y)], we note that in many practical settings, the true reward is either (i) binary or (ii) accessible only through (potentially noisy) pairwise comparisons. In the former case, expected true reward drastically simplifies to a search problem and is tightly analyzed in Huang et al. [14]. In the latter case, however, the expected numerical value of the reward is less meaningful as the learner will never have access to r⋆r^{\star} itself. Instead, we consider the win-rate induced by r⋆r^{\star} of the learned policy against the comparator policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, defined to be:

Rr⋆​(π)=ℙy∼π,y′∼πref​(r⋆​(y)>r⋆​(y′))+12⋅ℙy∼π,y′∼πref​(r⋆​(y)=r⋆​(y′)).\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi)=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(r^{\star}(y)>r^{\star}(y^{\prime}))+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(r^{\star}(y)=r^{\star}(y^{\prime})\right). (2)

More generally, r⋆r^{\star} could be replaced with another reward function, such as r^\widehat{r}, and (2) would define the win-rate under that reward function. We remark that while (2) uses the base model from which we draw candidate samples, πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, as the comparator policy, in principle one could evaluate win-rate against an arbitrary comparison distribution qq. This latter setting is relevant in practice, as it corresponds to AlpacaEval-style pipelines [8, 7] where qq corresponds to a strong comparator like GPT-4. For the sake of simplicity and clarity of presentation, we will first present our results for the special case where q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, and then show that for general qq, under natural closeness assumptions between qq and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, the same arguments yield qualitatively similar results, which we detail in Section 6. It is immediate that expected rewards coincide (up to a constant factor) with the notion of win rate in the special case where all reward functions are binary. Given a comparator policy π⋆\pi^{\star}, we wish to minimize the regret of a candidate policy π^\widehat{\pi}, i.e., Reg⁡(π^)=Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^)\reg(\widehat{\pi})=R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}). The fundamental question we ask is:

Within the sample-and-evaluate framework, how many samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} are necessary and sufficient to achieve low regret with respect to a given comparator policy π⋆\pi^{\star} and how should we select which output to return?

In order to answer this question, we have to better understand in what sense the reward model r^\widehat{r} is close to the true reward r⋆r^{\star} and in what sense the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is a good proxy for the comparator policy π⋆\pi^{\star}. We discuss these two questions in turn below.

2.2 In what sense is r^\widehat{r} close to r⋆r^{\star}?

Our first goal is to formalize the sense in which the learned reward model r^\widehat{r} is close to the true reward r⋆r^{\star}. Critically, the reward model r^\widehat{r} is trained on ‘typical’ outputs, which we formalize by assuming that r^\widehat{r} is close to r⋆r^{\star} on samples drawn from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. While Huang et al. [14] supposed that the squared error, εRM2​(r^)=𝔼y∼πref​[(r^​(y)−r⋆​(y))2]\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left(\widehat{r}(y)-r^{\star}(y)\right)^{2}\right] is small, we argue that this is not the most appropriate metric in our setting for two reasons. First, squared error is not scale-invariant, i.e., multiplying r^\widehat{r} by a positive constant does not change the behavior of any selection algorithm that uses r^\widehat{r} to select outputs, but it does change the squared error. Second, assuming small squared error is somewhat unnatural when rewards are only accessible through pairwise comparisons. Indeed, there is a philosophical point to be made here: if rewards are only accessible through pairwise comparisons, then it is not clear that there is any meaningful ground-truth numerical reward function r⋆r^{\star} at all beyond the ordinal information it induces. Numerical reward functions are often trained by running Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) on pairwise comparison data assuming the Bradley-Terry model [4, 27], which is known to suffer sample complexity scaling exponentially in the maximum reward value33 3 Indeed, it arises naturally as a simple calculation reveals that the maximum inverse Fisher information scales similarly. [28, 35]. Instead, we propose to measure the quality of r^\widehat{r} through its pairwise win-rate error with respect to r⋆r^{\star}:

εpw(r^):=𝔼y,y′∼πref[|ϕr^(y,y′)−ϕr⋆(y,y′)|]andϕr(y,y′):=𝟏{r(y)>r(y′)}+12 1{r(y)=r(y′)}\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}):=\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[|\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})|\right]\quad\text{and}\quad\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime}):=\mathbf{1}\{r(y)>r(y^{\prime})\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{r(y)=r(y^{\prime})\} (3)

Here, εpw​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) quantifies the amount by which r^\widehat{r} disagrees with r⋆r^{\star} on the outcome of two ‘typical’ responses sampled from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. In particular, the absolute difference |ϕr^​(y,y′)−ϕr⋆​(y,y′)||\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})| vanishes when r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} agree on the pairwise comparison outcome between yy and y′y^{\prime}, is 1/2\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} when one of the reward functions has a tie and the other does not, and penalizes disagreements between r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} that flip the win-versus-loss outcome with a full penalty of 11. This definition of εpw​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) is thus closely aligned wth the notion of win rate, which rewards strict wins more than ties. This alignment with the win-rate functional (which also half-counts ties and ranges between 00 and 11) hearkens back to our discussion on win-rate in Section 1 and will prove to be important in our later analyses.

This metric is clearly scale-invariant and more closely matches the way reward models are trained in practice [24, 27, 19], suggesting that (3) may be a more reasonable quantity to expect controlled than εRM2\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}. In the Bradley-Terry model, an elementary analysis shows that the tightest relationship between the two quantities scales exponentially in the maximum reward value, suggesting that when learning with finitely many samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, we may expect εpw​(r^)≪εRM2​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\ll\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r}). In general, however, εpw​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) is incomparable to εRM2​(r^)\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r}) as we show in Appendix A. Indeed, the scale invariance of εpw\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}} immediately implies that there are examples where εpw=0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}=0 but εRM2\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}} is arbitrary. Another sense in which requiring εRM2​(r^)\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r}) to be small is a stronger assumption than requiring εpw​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) to be small is that we cannot recover small regret in terms of expected true reward from small εpw​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) (cf. Proposition 3 in Appendix A), in marked contrast to small εpw​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) [14]; as we discussed above, in many situations, winrate is the more natural notion of reward.

2.3 In what sense is πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} a good reference model?

In addition to the quality of r^\widehat{r} as a proxy for r⋆r^{\star}, we must also consider the quality of the πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. Intuitively, if πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} places much less mass on high-reward outputs than the comparator policy π⋆\pi^{\star}, then NN must be very large in order to obtain comparable performance to the comparator. Thus, any notion of sample complexity must depend on some measure of discrepancy between π⋆\pi^{\star} and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. While prior work has supposed that Dχ2​(π⋆∥πref)\mathrm{D}_{\chi^{2}}\left(\pi^{\star}\middle\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right) is small, where we recall that Dχ2​(ν∥μ)=𝔼⁡[(d​ν/d​μ−1)2]\mathrm{D}_{\chi^{2}}\left(\nu\middle\|\mu\right)=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\nicefrac{{d\nu}}{{d\mu}}-1\right)^{2}\right] is the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence between two distributions ν\nu and μ\mu, this assumption is somewhat ad hoc. Indeed, the requirement of small Dχ2​(π⋆∥πref)\mathrm{D}_{\chi^{2}}\left(\pi^{\star}\middle\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right) falls directly out of the assumption that εRM2​(r^)\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r}) is small due to the duality between χ2\chi^{2}-divergence and squared error; thus while natural in that context, there is no a priori reason to prefer χ2\chi^{2}-divergence over any other discrepancy measure. We instead propose to measure this discrepancy through the fundamental notion of ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence [26, 2], where for any M≥0M\geq 0, we let

ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=𝔼y∼πref[(d​π⋆/d​πref(y)−M)+].\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left(\nicefrac{{d\pi^{\star}}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}(y)-M\right)_{+}\right]. (4)

While the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence has many applications [26, 25], its relevance here stems from the fact that Block and Polyanskiy [2] demonstrated its intimate connection to the problem of approximate sampling: in order to generate samples from a target distribution π⋆\pi^{\star} using only samples from a reference distribution πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} within tolerance (in total variation distance) ε\varepsilon, any algorithm requires at least MM samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, where ℰM(π⋆∥πref)≤ε\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\leq\varepsilon. Such a characterization is natural in the sample-and-evaluate framework of Definition 1 because a natural skyline for our setting would be to approximately sample from π⋆\pi^{\star} using samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and then return the sampled output, if the learner had access to knowledge of π⋆\pi^{\star} beyond that furnished by r^\widehat{r}. Moreover, the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence is intimately related to the recently introduced notion of coverage [6], which has been fruitfully applied to understand LMs in a variety of settings. Coverage measures the tail discrepancy between two distributions and is defined for M≥0M\geq 0 to be

CovM(π⋆∥πref)=ℙy∼π⋆(d​π⋆/d​πref(y)≥M).\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi^{\star}}\left(\nicefrac{{d\pi^{\star}}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}(y)\geq M\right). (5)

It is straightforward to see that ℰM(π⋆∥πref)≤CovM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\leq\mathrm{Cov}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) for all M≥0M\geq 0. More generally, ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence is a special case of ff-divergences [25], defined for convex f:ℝ≥0→ℝ≥0f:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} with f⁡(1)=f′​(1)=0f(1)=f^{\prime}(1)=0 to be

Df​(ν∥μ)=𝔼y∼μ​[f⁡(d​ν/d​μ​(y))].\displaystyle\mathrm{D}_{f}\left(\nu\middle\|\mu\right)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mu}\left[f\left(\nicefrac{{d\nu}}{{d\mu}}(y)\right)\right]. (6)

This family includes many well-known divergences, such as KL-divergence, Total Variation distance, and χ2\chi^{2}-divergence and a key result of Block and Polyanskiy [2] shows that for any such ff-divergence, we have ℰM(π⋆∥πref)≤M⋅Df​(π⋆∥πref)/f⁡(M)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\leq\nicefrac{{M\cdot\mathrm{D}_{f}\left(\pi^{\star}\middle\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)}}{{f(M)}}.

With these notions of reward model and reference model quality in place, we may now refine our central question to be:

Within the sample-and-evaluate framework, how many samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} are necessary and sufficient to achieve low regret with respect to a given comparator policy π⋆\pi^{\star} as a function of the pairwise win-rate error εpw​(r^)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) and ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})?

3 Optimal Performance with Best-of-NN

In this section we begin answering the question posed at the end of Section 2 by providing upper bounds on the win-rate regret achieved by the most naïve algorithm in the sample-and-evaluate framework, Best-of-NN (BoN):

π^BoN=argmaxy∈{y1,…,yN}r^​(y),yi∼πref.\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}=\argmax_{y\in\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\}}\widehat{r}(y),\quad y_{i}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. (7)

The BoN algorithm in (7), introduced in [29], simply pretends that r⋆=r^r^{\star}=\widehat{r} and returns the sample with the highest predicted reward among NN i.i.d. draws from the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. While BoN is susceptible to overoptimization, due to the fact that r^\widehat{r} may not approximate r⋆r^{\star} on typical outputs drawn from π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} even if it does so on typical outputs drawn from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, the algorithm has seen widespread practical use. We have the following upper bound on the performance.

Theorem 3.

For any N≥1N\geq 1, reference model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, comparator π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, ground truth reward r⋆r^{\star}, and learned reward model r^\widehat{r}, it holds that

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(π^BoN)≲N⋅εpw(r^)⋅log(1/εpw​(r^))+ℰN/log⁡(1/εpw​(r^))(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})\lesssim N\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\cdot\log\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})}}\right)+\mathcal{E}_{N/\log(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}))}\left(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right). (8)

There are two terms in the upper bound (8). The first term quantifies the degree to which reward hacking occurs: as NN increases, the algorithm is more likely to select outputs on which r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} disagree. The second term quantifies the extent to which, even if r^=r⋆\widehat{r}=r^{\star}, the BoN algorithm is able to find high-reward outputs comparable to those of the comparator π⋆\pi^{\star} using only samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}; here the ℰN\mathcal{E}_{N}-divergence naturally arises as the relevant measure of discrepancy between π⋆\pi^{\star} and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} due to the connection between ℰN\mathcal{E}_{N} and approximate rejection sampling outlined in Block and Polyanskiy [2]. Applying a key lemma from that work relating ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence to the ff-divergence (cf. Section 2), we may further bound (8) by N⋅εpw​(r^)+N⋅Df​(π⋆∥πref)/f⁡(N)N\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})+\nicefrac{{N\cdot\mathrm{D}_{f}\left(\pi^{\star}\middle\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)}}{{f(N)}}; in the special case of χ2\chi^{2}-divergence, tuning NN, we get (up to a log factor) an optimal rate of εpw(r^)⋅χ2(π⋆∥πref)\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\cdot\chi^{2}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})} of the regret, which bears at least cosmetic similarity to the results of Huang et al. [14], although we emphasize that here we are considering win rate as opposed to expected reward. In the special case of binary rewards, however, expected reward becomes a special case of win rate (cf. Section 2), and thus the above upper bound recovers the result of Huang et al. [14] in this setting.

In contradistinction to the case of expected reward, where BoN’s performance is suboptimal statistically, we find that BoN is in fact optimal for win-rate regret up to constant factors, as established by the following lower bound.

Theorem 4.

For any non-atomic πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, any π^𝒜\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{A}} in the sample-and-evaluate framework, and any ε<1/2\varepsilon<\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}, there exist reward functions r^\widehat{r}, r⋆r^{\star} satisfying εpw​(r^)≤ε\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\leq\varepsilon and a comparator policy π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} for which

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(π^𝒜)≳infM{M⋅ε+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)}.\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{A}})\gtrsim\inf_{M}\left\{M\cdot\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\right\}. (9)

This result shows that unlike in the expected-reward setting, BoN is in fact optimal up to a logarithmic factor for win-rate regret within the sample-and-evaluate framework, which helps explain its widespread practical use despite its simplicity. This observation gently pushes back against the conclusion reached by Huang et al. [14] that observed that, when optimizing for expected reward, BoN is statistically suboptimal and more sophisticated algorithms are necessary to achieve optimal performance. As we have emphasized repeatedly, however, we believe that win rate is often a more natural objective than expected reward in many practical settings, and thus the suggestion that BoN should be avoided for being statistically suboptimal may be overstated. In addition to the statistical lower bound above, we also provide a complementary computational lower bound.

Proposition 1.

For any M≥2M\geq 2 and δ<1/2\delta<\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}, there exist reward functions r⋆=r^r^{\star}=\widehat{r} and policies π⋆,πref\pi^{\star},\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} with ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0 such that within the sample-and-evaluate framework, any policy π^\widehat{\pi} achieving regret Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^)≤δR^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi})\leq\delta must use at least N=Ω~​(M)N=\widetilde{\Omega}(M) samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}.

This bound is computational in the sense that if we did not care about computational efficiency (quantified by NN in the sample-and-evaluate framework), then it is trivial to achieve small regret with π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}, as r^=r⋆\widehat{r}=r^{\star}; on the other hand, if we want to achieve small regret, then we have a strong lower bound on the number of samples required. We emphasize that this lower bound matches the upper bound of Theorem 3 and thus BoN is computationally and statistically optimal for win-rate regret within the sample-and-evaluate framework.

4 Achieving Optimal Performance without Reward-Hacking

While in the previous section we saw that the naïve Best-of-NN algorithm given in (7) is computationally and statistically optimal for win-rate regret with optimally tuned NN, it is still susceptible to reward-hacking. That is, as NN increases, the algorithm is more likely to select outputs on which r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} disagree, leading to performance that scales non-monotonically in NN. While understandable, this is an unfortunate property, as in practice one would like to be able to increase NN to improve performance without worrying about overfitting to the reward proxy r^\widehat{r}. In this section, we present a new algorithm, ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized Best-of-NN, that is able to mitigate reward-hacking and achieve performance that is monotone in NN while still being statistically and computationally optimal.

Intuitively, we would like a policy that returns high-reward outputs without straying too far from the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, as outputs that are unlikely under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} are more likely to be subject to reward-hacking. Our analysis and results from the previous section suggest that the appropriate way to measure discrepancy from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is via the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence for an appropriate choice of MM, defined in (4). Motivated by this observation, we consider the following variational problem:

πM∈argmaxπ𝔼π[r^(y)]−Rmax⋅ℰM(π∥πref),\displaystyle\pi_{M}\in\argmax_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\widehat{r}(y)\right]-R_{\mathrm{max}}\cdot\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), (10)

whose solution we refer to as the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized Best-of-NN policy. Note that it is perhaps not immediate that (10) is a desirable objective to consider; indeed, while a similar objective, with ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M} replaced by χ2\chi^{2}, was considered by Huang et al. [14] in the context of expected reward maximization, in our setting we do not care about the expected reward per se, but rather the win-rate. Another potential concern is that the variational problem in (10) is not easily sampled from within the sample-and-evaluate framework, as it is not immediately clear how to draw samples from the optimal policy πM\pi_{M}. The second concern is allayed, however, by the following result, which shows that the optimal policy for (10) takes a particularly simple form.

Lemma 1.

Let λ\lambda be the (1−1/M)(1-\nicefrac{{1}}{{M}})-quantile of r^\widehat{r} under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, i.e. any value satisfying ℙ​(r^​(y)≥λ)=1/M\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda\right)=\nicefrac{{1}}{{M}}. Then the optimal policy πM\pi_{M} solving (10) is given by πM(⋅)=πref(⋅∣r^(⋅)≥λ)\pi_{M}(\cdot)=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid\widehat{r}(\cdot)\geq\lambda).

Remark 1.

One might instead consider a different variation of (10), where RmaxR_{\mathrm{max}} is replaced by a general scaling parameter β>0\beta>0. If β≥Rmax\beta\geq R_{\mathrm{max}} then this will end up having the same solution, but if β<Rmax\beta<R_{\mathrm{max}} then the solution can grow more complicated.

Lemma 1 is proved in Section D.1, where we use Lagrange multipliers and convexity to derive a remarkably simple characterization of the optimal policy. Note that πM\pi_{M} can be approximately sampled from within the sample-and-evaluate framework by drawing NN samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and returning a sample uniform from the top-⌈N/M⌉\lceil\nicefrac{{N}}{{M}}\rceil samples according to r^\widehat{r} with randomized tie-breaking (cf. Appendix D); indeed, the total variation distance between this sampling procedure and πM\pi_{M} is bounded by 1/N\nicefrac{{1}}{{N}} and π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} can be interpreted as doing BoN for N≲MN\lesssim M, but maintaining monotonicity as NN grows. We should emphasize that, in contrast to the procedure of Huang et al. [14], π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} is much simpler and does not require any additional estimation or rejection sampling. We have the following bound on the performance of this variant, which we call π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M}.

Theorem 5.

For any M,N≥1M,N\geq 1, reference model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, comparator π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, ground truth reward r⋆r^{\star}, and learned reward model r^\widehat{r}, it holds that

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(π^M)≲ℰM(π⋆∥πref)+M⋅εpw+1N,\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\lesssim\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+M\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}+\frac{1}{N}, (11)

Note that the upper bound in (11) is very similar to that of BoN in Theorem 3, with the key difference being that the scaling parameter NN is now decoupled from the regularization parameter MM. As a result, by tuning MM appropriately, we can achieve the performance skyline established in Theorem 3 while maintaining monotonicity in NN. Other than monotonicity, the monotone algorithm performs similarly to BoN and we note that it still requires tuning of the regularization parameter MM, so we expect BoN to remain the dominant alignment algorithm when monotonicity is not required.

We conclude this section by observing that the only prior provably monotone algorithm, the χ2\chi^{2}-regularized Best-of-NN algorithm proposed by Huang et al. [14], can fail to achieve optimal performance when win-rate regret is the goal. Specifically, we have the following result.

Proposition 2 (Separation between πβχ\pi^{\chi}_{\beta} vs πM\pi_{M}).

For every c>1c>1, there exist policies πref,π⋆\pi_{\mathrm{ref}},\pi^{\star}, reward functions r^,r⋆\widehat{r},r^{\star}, and εpw≪1\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}\ll 1 such that εpw​(r^)≤εpw\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}} and it holds that

infβ>0Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(πβχ)≥c⋅(infM>0Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(πM)).\displaystyle\inf_{\beta>0}R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\chi}_{\beta})\geq c\cdot\left(\inf_{M>0}R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\pi_{M})\right). (12)

This result, whose proof is deferred to Section D.3, demonstrates that the χ2\chi^{2}-regularized Best-of-NN algorithm can perform much worse than our proposed algorithm. In addition to the poor performance demonstrated in Proposition 2, we emphasize that one of the chief advantages of the algorithm proposed in this section over that of πβχ\pi^{\chi}_{\beta} and alternatives such as soft-BoN [17, 31], running BoN with pessimistic reward estimates, and alternatives [16] is in its simplicity: the optimal policy takes the form of a simple top-quantile selector, which is easy to implement and sample from in practice and requires no online estimation or additional computational overhead.

5 Proof Techniques

Next, we provide proof sketches of our main results on the performance of BoN under win-rate regret (Theorems 3 and 4) and an upper bound for the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized algorithm (Theorem 5).

5.1 Proof Sketch of Theorem 3

In order to compare the performance of π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} to that of an arbitrary comparator policy π⋆\pi^{\star} under the true reward function r⋆r^{\star}, we need to overcome two main challenges: (1) if NN is too small and π⋆\pi^{\star} is far from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, then we could pay in regret for not being able to find high-reward outputs comparable to those of π⋆\pi^{\star}; and (2) if NN is too large, then we may overoptimize r^\widehat{r} and select outputs on which r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} disagree. This tension is captured by the two terms in the upper bound (8), which arise out of the following regret decomposition holding for any M>0M>0: the regret Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^BoN)R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}) is equal to the sum of three terms,

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)⏟(i)+Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)⏟(ii)+Rr^​(π^BoN)−Rr⋆​(π^BoN)⏟(iii),\displaystyle\underbrace{R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})}_{\text{(i)}}+\underbrace{R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})}_{\text{(ii)}}+\underbrace{R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})}_{\text{(iii)}}, (13)

where πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} is an intermediate comparator policy defined to be the policy that minimizes total variation distance to π⋆\pi^{\star} subject to the constraint that its density ratio relative to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is upper bounded by MM almost surely. While a similar decomposition was introduced in Huang et al. [14], the key challenge in our setting is that we are considering win-rate regret rather than expected-reward regret, which requires different techniques to control each of the terms in (13).

Term (i).

We further decompose

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M}) =Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(πM⋆)+Rr⋆​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)\displaystyle=R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})+R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M}) (14)

and control each of the two resulting differences separately. For the first difference, we observe that win-rate is bounded and thus 11-Lipschitz in total variation distance, so we can control the loss from π⋆\pi^{\star} to πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} in terms of ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) by Block and Polyanskiy [2]. For the second difference, we use the fact that the likelihood ratio of πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is upper bounded by MM almost surely to control the pairwise win-rate error under πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} between r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} by M⋅εpw​(r^)M\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) using change-of-measure.

Term (ii).

Here, we again adopt the formalism of approximate rejection sampling from Block and Polyanskiy [2] to define a selection rule to be a policy πM,rej⋆\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}} that approximates πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} using only NN i.i.d. draws from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. We again further decompose term (ii) as

Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)=Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM,rej⋆)+Rr^​(πM,rej⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})=R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}})+R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}) (15)

and control each of the two resulting terms separately. For the first difference, we use the approximate rejection sampling analysis of Block and Polyanskiy [2] to show that πM,rej⋆\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}} approximates πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} in total variation distance up to an exponentially small term in N/MN/M, which again transfers to win-rate by boundedness. For the second term, we observe that conditional on any fixed batch of NN samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, BoN simply selects the output with the highest r^\widehat{r} value, and thus dominates any other selection rule on that same batch under r^\widehat{r}, including πM,rej⋆\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}}; while this fact is intuitively true, we prove it rigorously in Appendix C.

Term (iii).

Finally, we control term (iii) using a similar change-of-measure argument as for term (i), observing that BoN has density ratio at most NN relative to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} almost surely and thus the pairwise win rate error under π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} between r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} is at most N⋅εpw​(r^)N\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}).

Conclusion.

Combining the bounds for terms (i), (ii), and (iii) yields, for any M>0M>0,

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(π^BoN)≲(M+N)⋅εpw(r^)+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)+exp(−N/M).\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})\lesssim(M+N)\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+\exp(-N/M). (16)

Setting M=N/log⁡(1/εpw​(r^))M=N/\log(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})) then gives the desired upper bound.

5.2 Proof Sketch of Theorem 4

Prior lower bounds for expected-reward regret [14] do not directly apply to win-rate regret, as they rely on constructing reward functions that differ on a small set of outputs with low probability under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} but high expected reward, which does not affect win rate significantly. Indeed, it is precisely because such constructions do not seriously affect win rate that BoN is able to achieve optimal performance for win-rate regret, in contrast to expected-reward regret. For fixed π^\widehat{\pi}, πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, and r^\widehat{r}, we construct a family of rA⋆r^{\star}_{A} parameterized by measurable subsets A⊆𝒴A\subseteq\mathcal{Y} such that rA⋆r^{\star}_{A} differs from r^\widehat{r} only on AA, i.e., r⋆​(y)=r^​(y)+𝕀​y∈Ar^{\star}(y)=\widehat{r}(y)+\mathbb{I}{y\in A}. A computation shows that

εpw​(r^)≤πref​(A)⋅(1−πref​(A))≤πref​(A),\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\leq\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)\cdot(1-\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A))\leq\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A), (17)

so by choosing AA to have πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-measure at most ε\varepsilon, we ensure that the pairwise win rate error is small. A calculation tells us that with an appropriate choice of r^\widehat{r}, we can lower bound

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^)≳π⋆​(A)−π^​(A)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi})\gtrsim\pi^{\star}(A)-\widehat{\pi}(A) (18)

for any rA⋆r^{\star}_{A} in the family. Thus, the regret is large if, subject to πref​(A)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A) being small, we can ensure that π⋆​(A)\pi^{\star}(A) is large while π^​(A)\widehat{\pi}(A) is small. We apply Markov’s inequality to show that

π^​(d​π^d​πref≤2)≥12\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}\left(\frac{d\widehat{\pi}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\leq 2\right)\geq\frac{1}{2} (19)

and then use the non-atomicity of πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} to demonstrate the existence of an AA such that πref​(A)≤ε\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)\leq\varepsilon and π^​(A)≤2​ε\widehat{\pi}(A)\leq 2\varepsilon. We then choose π⋆\pi^{\star} such that d​π⋆/d​πref=M\nicefrac{{d\pi^{\star}}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}=M on AA and some small constant elsewhere to ensure that π⋆\pi^{\star} is a valid probability measure. For an appropriate choice of MM, we can use this instance to establish the lower bound.

5.3 Proof Sketch of Theorem 5

We begin in a similar way as the proof of Theorem 3 by considering a regret decomposition, i.e., the regret Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^M)R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}) is equal to

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^M)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}) =(Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆))⏟(i)+(Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^M))⏟(ii)+(Rr^​(π^M)−Rr⋆​(π^M))⏟(iii),\displaystyle=\underbrace{\big(R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\big)}_{\text{(i)}}+\underbrace{\big(R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\big)}_{\text{(ii)}}+\underbrace{\big(R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\big)}_{\text{(iii)}}, (20)

where πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} is the same as that defined in Section 5.1. As such, term (i) is handled exactly as in the BoN proof, contributing ℰM(π⋆∥πref)+M⋅εpw(r^)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+M\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}). Similarly, term (iii) is also handled in the same way as in the BoN proof, except we have that π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} has density ratio at most MM relative to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} almost surely (not increasing with NN, in contradistinction to BoN). It remains to control term (ii). We now decompose

Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^M)=Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM)+Rr^​(πM)−Rr^​(π^M),\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})=R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})+R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}), (21)

where πM\pi_{M} samples uniformly from the top 1/M\nicefrac{{1}}{{M}} quantile of r^​(y)\widehat{r}(y) for y∼πrefy\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. The first difference is non-positive by a similar argument as in the BoN analysis (cf. Section D.2). To bound the second difference, we compute the win-rate of the empirical quantile policy π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} and the population quantile policy πM\pi_{M} explicitly: after tie-breaking, the r^\widehat{r}-ranks of the NN samples are i.i.d. Unif⁡[0,1]\mathrm{Unif}[0,1], so the win-rate of π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} admits an explicit order statistic formula, yielding Rr^​(π^M)≥1−1/2​M−1/NR^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\geq 1-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2M}}-\nicefrac{{1}}{{N}}, while Rr^​(πM)=1−1/2​MR^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})=1-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2M}}, so the difference is at most 1/N\nicefrac{{1}}{{N}}. The result follows.

6 Performance Under Win-rate Against an Arbitrary Policy

In this section, we extend our performance guarantees for BoN and ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized BoN to the setting where win-rate is evaluated against an arbitrary comparison policy qq (rather than the baseline q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} used in Equation 2) as discussed in Section 2.1. This generality aligns with common evaluation pipelines—for example, in AlpacaEval-style benchmarks [8, 7] one often measures win-rate against a strong comparator like GPT-4. Formally, for any comparison measure qq on 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and any reward function rr, we define the win-rate against qq by

Rqr(π):=𝔼y∼π,y′∼q[ϕr(y,y′)]andϕr(y,y′):=𝟏{r(y)>r(y′)}+12 1{r(y)=r(y′)}.\displaystyle R^{r}_{q}(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi,\;y^{\prime}\sim q}\!\left[\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime})\right]\quad\text{and}\quad\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime}):=\mathbf{1}\{r(y)>r(y^{\prime})\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{r(y)=r(y^{\prime})\}. (22)

This definition generalizes the win-rate in Equation 2 (which corresponds to q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) by drawing y′∼qy^{\prime}\sim q as the baseline comparator. Throughout this section we assume that qq is dominated by πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} (q≪πrefq\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) with a pointwise density-ratio bound

wq​(y):=d​qd​πref​(y)≤Lπref​-a.s.,\displaystyle w_{q}(y):=\frac{dq}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)\leq L\quad\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\text{-a.s.}, (23)

for some constant L≥1L\geq 1. This condition lets us relate win-rate against qq to quantities (such as pairwise error and excess mass) that are defined with respect to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} via the same change-of-measure steps as in Sections 5.1 and 5.3, up to a multiplicative factor LL. One could instead work with a weaker divergence control, e.g. ℰL(q∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{L}(q\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), but we use (23) to keep the bookkeeping minimal. We continue to measure pairwise reward-model error with respect to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} via

εpw​(r^)=𝔼y,y′∼πref​[|ϕr^​(y,y′)−ϕr⋆​(y,y′)|].\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[\big|\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})\big|\right]. (24)

The following result extends our BoN guarantee from the baseline comparison q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} to an arbitrary comparison measure qq satisfying (23).

Theorem 6.

Suppose that πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and qq satisfy (23) and let π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. Then for any reward models r⋆r^{\star} and r^\widehat{r} and any N≥1N\geq 1, it holds that

Rqr⋆(π⋆)−Rqr⋆(π^BoN)≲L⋅N⋅εpw(r^)⋅log(1/εpw​(r^))+ℰN/log⁡(1/εpw​(r^))(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle R_{q}^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R_{q}^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})\lesssim L\cdot N\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\cdot\log\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})}}\right)+\mathcal{E}_{N/\log(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}))}\left(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right). (25)

Theorem 6 recovers Theorem 3 in the case that q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}; more generally, we pay in regret for the mismatch between reference model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and comparator qq through the uniform density ratio bound. This factor arises because the regret decomposition and subsequent change-of-measure steps are identical to the q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} case (cf. Section 5.1), except that expectations against y′∼qy^{\prime}\sim q are controlled by expectations against y′∼πrefy^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} using (23). The remaining terms are bounded by the same approximate rejection sampling arguments from Block and Polyanskiy [2], so BoN remains statistically and computationally optimal under win-rate regret, while still being susceptible to reward hacking through εpw\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}. As discussed in Section 4, ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized BoN overcomes this issue and decouples the scaling parameter NN from the regularization parameter MM and yields a monotone-in-NN guarantee for q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}; in the next theorem we extend an analogous guarantee for π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} to general qq under (23).

Theorem 7.

For any M,N≥1M,N\geq 1, reference model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, comparator π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, ground truth reward r⋆r^{\star}, and learned reward model r^\widehat{r}, it holds that

Rqr⋆(π⋆)−Rqr⋆(π^M)≲L⋅ℰM(π⋆∥πref)+L⋅M⋅εpw(r^)+MN.\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}_{q}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}_{q}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\lesssim L\cdot\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+L\cdot M\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})+\sqrt{\frac{M}{N}}. (26)

Once again, we recover the case where q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} from Theorem 5 by setting L=1L=1, except we now have introduced an additional term that decays as M/N\sqrt{M/N}. We emphasize that this is purely a computationaly phenomenon as, taking N↑∞N\uparrow\infty, we recover the same statistical rate as in Best-of-N above. In the special case when q=πrefq=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, the win-rate of a top-1/M1/M quantile policy under r^\widehat{r} admits an explicit order-statistics calculation, yielding a fast 1/N1/N dependence. For a general qq, the same top-quantile selection step must be analyzed through how qq places mass across r^\widehat{r}-level sets near the cutoff; without additional structure, qq may concentrate its probability mass in a narrow band of scores around the quantile threshold, making the win-rate highly sensitive to small fluctuations in the empirical cutoff induced by a finite batch of NN samples. Thus, we control this step using concentration of empirical quantiles, which leads to the slower rate in NN. Finally, we note that the density-ratio bound in (23) is only one convenient way to relate win-rate against qq to quantities defined with respect to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. We leave to future work the interesting question of the extent to which such a term is necessary in the general-qq setting, and whether one can recover a faster rate under additional regularity assumptions on qq.

7 Discussion and Related Work

In this work, we studied the problem of inference-time alignment within the sample-and-evaluate framework, focusing on the widely used Best-of-NN (BoN) algorithm. In contradistinction to prior work that focused on expected true reward as the objective of interest, we argued that win rate is often a more natural objective in practical settings where reward models are trained and evaluated using pairwise comparisons. We demonstrated that BoN is both statistically and computationally optimal within the sample-and-evaluate framework for achieving good win rate, partially explaining its widespread practical success despite its simplicity. Because BoN remains susceptible to reward-hacking even under the win-rate objective, we proposed a simple variant that provably eliminates reward-hacking while maintaining optimal statistical performance. Our work suggests several interesting directions for future research. First, we may ask if there is a unifying paradigm that captures both expected-reward and win-rate objectives as special cases, allowing us to better understand under what conditions (optimally tuned) BoN is optimal and when more sophisticated algorithms are necessary. Second, while we have focused on the sample-and-evaluate framework as a natural abstraction of inference-time alignment, it would be interesting to understand if similar statistical and computational guarantees can be achieved in more general frameworks that allow for adaptive sampling or other forms of interaction with the reference model. Finally, while our proposed variant of BoN eliminates reward-hacking in theory, it may still be too conservative in practice due to its reliance on information-theoretic guarantees; moving beyond such guarantees and leveraging the rich structure that learned representations provide in order to improve inference-time alignment remains an interesting question. We now discuss several related works in more detail.

Inference-time Alignment.

Inference time alignment is a popular framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences without requiring expensive retraining [29, 23, 34, 24, 13, 11]. Both inference and training time alignment typically targets skills in reasoning, knowledge, or value alignment [15, 12, 24, 5], and has been successfully applied to a variety of tasks. The former domains often involve binary rewards, where an answer is either true or not, while the latter often involves more subjective human preferences that generally are measured through win rate [20, 8, 7, 24]. Our work focuses on the latter setting, where win rate is a more natural objective than expected reward.

Best-of-NN.

When the learner has access to a groundtruth verifier, Brown et al. [5] demonstrated that simply running a Best-of-NN (BoN) procedure with samples from the base model and selecting the output with the highest true reward is effective at producing high-quality outputs in a range of tasks. In practice, however, the groundtruth reward is not accessible, and instead a learned reward model is used to select among samples from the base model [29, 24, 1]. While BoN with a learned reward model has seen widespread practical use, it is vulnerable to reward-hacking, which has been extensively explored [9, 30]. A number of ad hoc empirical mitigation attempts have been proposed, including regularization in representation space [16], a pessimistic BoN using empirical uncertainty quantification, and a KL-regularized variant of BoN [31, 17]. None of these approaches have theoretical guarantees that improve substantially over BoN. On the theoretical side, the most relevant work is that of Huang et al. [14], which analyzed BoN under the expected-reward objective and demonstrated that it is statistically suboptimal in general due to its vulnerability to reward overoptimization. They then proposed a more sophisticated algorithm that achieves optimal statistical performance by leveraging ideas from approximate rejection sampling [2]. In contradistinction to their work, we demonstrated that BoN is in fact statistically and computationally optimal under the win-rate objective, which we believe is often more natural in practice. Thus, while conceptually similar, our results paint a more favorable picture of BoN than that of Huang et al. [14] and our techniques (in particular our lower bounds) differ significantly.

Appendix A Investigation of Different Notions of Error and Performance

In this section, we demonstrate that the pairwise error and squared error as defined in Section 2.2 are generally incomparable. In particular, Lemma 2 shows that small εpw\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}} does not imply small εRM2\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}, while Lemma 3 shows the converse. In addition, we provide a proof of Proposition 3, which shows the impossibility of bounding expected reward regret as a function of the pairwise error and excess mass divergence introduced in Section 2.3 uniformly across all problems.

A.1 Proofs for Reward Model Error Comparison

Fix a base policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. For all c>0c>0 there are unbounded reward models r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} with

Pairwise error lower bound.

Recall the pairwise outcome

ϕr(y,y′)=𝟏{r(y)>r(y′)}+12 1{r(y)=r(y′)},\displaystyle\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime})=\mathbf{1}\{r(y)>r(y^{\prime})\}+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{r(y)=r(y^{\prime})\}, (38)

A.2 Proof of Proposition 3

To construct a lower bound on expected reward regret, we will make r^\widehat{r} assign the same maximal score to a high-scoring region SS of πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-mass 1/M1/M, so that any alignment algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} has no information to distinguish points inside SS and can only pick some distribution over SS. We then define r⋆r^{\star} to place all its value on the part of SS that 𝒜\mathcal{A} selects least (while keeping εpw\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}} and ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) small), forcing a large true-reward regret. For completeness, we first restate the theorem before providing a proof.

Proposition 3.

Fix a threshold M≥2M\geq 2. For any inference-time algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} and for every ε∈(0,1/M)\varepsilon\in(0,1/M) there exists an instance with unbounded rewards (πref,r^,r⋆)(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}},\widehat{r},r^{\star}) and a comparator policy π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} such that

εpw≤εandℰM(π⋆∥πref)=εM,\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}\leq\ \varepsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\varepsilon M, (49)

while, for every target gap γ>0\gamma>0,

𝔼π⋆​[r⋆]−𝔼π𝒜​[r⋆]≥γ.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}}[r^{\star}]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathcal{A}}}[r^{\star}]\ \geq\ \gamma. (50)

By taking ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, one can make the regret arbitrarily large while simultaneously having εpw→0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}\to 0 and ℰM(π⋆∥πref)→0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\to 0.

Proof.

Define α:=1/M\alpha:=1/M. We construct πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} to be non-atomic and supported on two disjoint measurable regions BB and SS with πref​(S)=α\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(S)=\alpha and πref​(B)=1−α\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(B)=1-\alpha. Precisely, let BB and SS be disjoint measurable sets, each equipped with a non-atomic probability measure. Define the reward model

r^​(y)=0​for ​y∈B,r^​(y)=Rmax​for ​y∈S.\displaystyle\widehat{r}(y)=0\ \text{for }y\in B,\qquad\widehat{r}(y)=R_{\max}\ \text{for }y\in S. (51)

Let π𝒜\pi_{\mathcal{A}} denote the (possibly randomized) policy output by 𝒜\mathcal{A} when run on input (πref,r^)(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}},\widehat{r}). Fix ε∈(0,α)\varepsilon\in(0,\alpha). Because r^\widehat{r} is constant on SS, the algorithm has no score-based signal to distinguish points within SS and may concentrate arbitrarily on some subset of SS. We therefore choose a region P⊆SP\subseteq S adversarially as an ε\varepsilon-mass subset that captures as much of π𝒜\pi_{\mathcal{A}}’s mass as possible:

P∈argsup{π𝒜(A):A⊆S,πref(A)=ε}.\displaystyle P\in\arg\sup\Big\{\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(A):A\subseteq S,\ \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)=\varepsilon\Big\}. (52)

Note that because πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is non-atomic and πref​(S)=α\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(S)=\alpha, there exist measurable subsets of SS of any prescribed πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-mass in [0,α][0,\alpha]. An exact maximizer need not exist; any PP achieving the supremum up to an arbitrarily small slack suffices. Also, define C:=S∖PC:=S\setminus P as well, so πref​(C)=α−ε\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(C)=\alpha-\varepsilon. Since PP is (approximately) maximal among ε\varepsilon-mass subsets of SS, its π𝒜\pi_{\mathcal{A}}-mass is at least the average π𝒜\pi_{\mathcal{A}}-mass over an ε/α\varepsilon/\alpha fraction of SS:

π𝒜​(P)≥πref​(P)πref​(S)​π𝒜​(S)=(ε​M)​π𝒜​(S).\displaystyle\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(P)\ \geq\ \frac{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(P)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(S)}\,\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(S)\ =\ (\varepsilon M)\,\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(S). (53)

Now we can let the true reward be maximized on the rest of SS by setting

r⋆(y):=cr^(y) 1{y∈C}={c​Rmax,y∈C,0,y∈B∪P,\displaystyle r^{\star}(y):=c\,\widehat{r}(y)\,\mathbf{1}\{y\in C\}=\begin{cases}cR_{\max},&y\in C,\\ 0,&y\in B\cup P,\end{cases} (54)

for some c>0c>0 to be chosen later, so that π⋆:=πref(⋅|C)\pi^{\star}:=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|\,C) and then 𝔼π⋆​[r⋆]=c​Rmax\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}}[r^{\star}]=cR_{\max}. Next, we compute ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). The density ratio w⋆=d​π⋆d​πrefw^{\star}=\frac{d\pi^{\star}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} equals 1πref​(C)=1α−ε\frac{1}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(C)}=\frac{1}{\alpha-\varepsilon} on CC and 00 elsewhere. Since M=1/αM=1/\alpha, we have w⋆>Mw^{\star}>M on CC, and therefore

ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) =𝔼πref​[(w⋆−M)+]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big[(w^{\star}-M)_{+}\big] (55)
=πref​(C)​(1πref​(C)−M)\displaystyle=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(C)\Big(\frac{1}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(C)}-M\Big) (56)
=ε​M.\displaystyle=\varepsilon M. (57)

ϕr(y,y′)=𝟏{r(y)>r(y′)}+12 1{r(y)=r(y′)}\displaystyle\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime})=\mathbf{1}\{r(y)>r(y^{\prime})\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{r(y)=r(y^{\prime})\} (58)

and the pairwise error

εpw​(r^)=𝔼y,y′∼πref​[|ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−ϕr^​(y,y′)|].\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})=\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left|\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})\right|\right]. (59)

In all these cases, |ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−ϕr^​(y,y′)|=12|\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})|=\tfrac{1}{2}. Therefore,

=12⋅2​πref​(P)​(1−πref​(P))\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(P)\left(1-\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(P)\right) (61)
=ε⁡(1−ε)≤ε.\displaystyle=\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)\leq\varepsilon. (62)

π𝒜​(P)≥πref​(P)πref​(S)​π𝒜​(S)=(ε​M)​π𝒜​(S),\displaystyle\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(P)\ \geq\ \frac{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(P)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(S)}\,\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(S)\ =\ (\varepsilon M)\,\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(S), (63)

Then, since r⋆r^{\star} is c​RmaxcR_{\max} on C=S∖PC=S\setminus P and 00 elsewhere,
