Appendix B Supporting Lemmas

The lemmas in this section provide key auxiliary results used throughout the rest of the proofs. Lemma 4 quantifies the win-rate penalty incurred when transferring between reward models, and provides good intuition for maneuvering the regret decomposition in the upper bounds. It is here where the alignment between the pairwise error and win-rate defintions is useful: we can translate control of pairwise outcome disagreements into control of win-rate differences. Lemma 5 demonstrates the relationship between our win-rate metric and the expected quantile under r^\widehat{r} achieved by a policy under a fixed reward model.

Lemma 4.

Fix a reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, a true reward r⋆r^{\star}, and a learned reward model r^\widehat{r}. For any policy π≪πref\pi\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} with density ratio wπ:=d​π/d​πrefw_{\pi}:=\nicefrac{{d\pi}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}} and any M≥1M\geq 1,

|Rr⋆(π)−Rr^(π)|≤M⋅εpw(r^)+ℰM(π∥πref).\displaystyle\left|R^{r^{\star}}(\pi)-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)\right|\;\leq\;M\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\;+\;\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (69)
Proof.

For any score function rr, we defined the pairwise outcome

ϕr(y,y′)=𝟏{r(y)>r(y′)}+12 1{r(y)=r(y′)}∈{0,12,1}.\displaystyle\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime})=\mathbf{1}\{r(y)>r(y^{\prime})\}+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{r(y)=r(y^{\prime})\}\in\left\{0,\frac{1}{2},1\right\}. (70)

Then by definition, the win-rate functional can be written as

Rr​(π)=𝔼y∼π,y′∼πref​[ϕr​(y,y′)].\displaystyle R^{r}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi,\;y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime})\right]. (71)

In addition, recall the pairwise error

εpw​(r^)=𝔼y,y′∼πref​[|ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−ϕr^​(y,y′)|].\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})=\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[|\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})|\right]. (72)

In order to bound the win-rate difference, we first observe that

|Rr⋆​(π)−Rr^​(π)|\displaystyle\left|R^{r^{\star}}(\pi)-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)\right| =|𝔼y∼π,y′∼πref​[ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−ϕr^​(y,y′)]|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi,\;y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})\right]\right| (73)
≤𝔼y∼π,y′∼πref​[|ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−ϕr^​(y,y′)|].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi,\;y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left|\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})\right|\right]. (74)

For shorthand, let ℓ⁡(y,y′)=|ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−ϕr^​(y,y′)|\ell(y,y^{\prime})=\left|\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})\right|. We can change measure using wπw_{\pi}:

𝔼y∼π,y′∼πref​[ℓ⁡(y,y′)]=𝔼y∼πref,y′∼πref​[wπ​(y)​ℓ​(y,y′)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi,\;y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\ell(y,y^{\prime})\right]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}},\;y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[w_{\pi}(y)\,\ell(y,y^{\prime})\right]. (75)

Then, we can decompose wπ​(y)=(wπ​(y)∧M)+(wπ​(y)−M)+w_{\pi}(y)=(w_{\pi}(y)\wedge M)+(w_{\pi}(y)-M)_{+} and use ℓ∈[0,1]\ell\in[0,1]:

𝔼y,y′∼πref​[wπ​(y)​ℓ​(y,y′)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[w_{\pi}(y)\ell(y,y^{\prime})\right] =𝔼y,y′∼πref​[(wπ​(y)∧M)​ℓ​(y,y′)]+𝔼y,y′∼πref​[(wπ​(y)−M)+​ℓ​(y,y′)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[(w_{\pi}(y)\wedge M)\,\ell(y,y^{\prime})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[(w_{\pi}(y)-M)_{+}\,\ell(y,y^{\prime})\right] (76)
≤M⋅𝔼y,y′∼πref​[ℓ⁡(y,y′)]+𝔼y∼πref​[(wπ​(y)−M)+]\displaystyle\leq M\cdot\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\ell(y,y^{\prime})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[(w_{\pi}(y)-M)_{+}\right] (77)
=M⋅εpw(r^)+ℰM(π∥πref).\displaystyle=M\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (78)

∎

Lemma 5.

Fix a reward model r^:𝒴→ℝ\widehat{r}:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}. Define the mid-CDF transform

F~r^​(t):=12​(Fr^​(t−)+Fr^​(t))∈[0,1].\displaystyle\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(t)\;:=\;\frac{1}{2}\left(F_{\widehat{r}}(t^{-})+F_{\widehat{r}}(t)\right)\in[0,1]. (79)

where

Fr^​(t):=ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y′)≤t),Fr^​(t−):=ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y′)<t).\displaystyle F_{\widehat{r}}(t)\;:=\;\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\leq t\right),\qquad F_{\widehat{r}}(t^{-})\;:=\;\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})<t\right). (80)

Then for any policy π\pi,

Rr^​(π)=𝔼y∼π​[F~r^​(r^​(y))],\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}\Big[\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)\right)\Big], (81)

Moreover, let V∼Unif⁡[0,1]V\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] be independent of everything, and define the randomized uniformized score

u~​(y):=Fr^​(r^​(y)−)+V⋅(Fr^​(r^​(y))−Fr^​(r^​(y)−))∈[0,1].\displaystyle\tilde{u}(y)\;:=\;F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\;+\;V\cdot\left(F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))-F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\right)\in[0,1]. (82)

Then:

  1. 1.

    For any π\pi, Rr^​(π)=𝔼y∼π,V​[u~​(y)]R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi,V}\big[\tilde{u}(y)\big].

  2. 2.

    If y′∼πrefy^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, then u~​(y′)∼Unif⁡[0,1]\tilde{u}(y^{\prime})\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1].

Proof.

By the law of total expectation,

Rr^​(π)=𝔼y∼π​[ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y)>r^​(y′)∣y)+12​ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y)=r^​(y′)∣y)].\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}\!\Big[\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\mid y\right)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\mid y\right)\Big]. (83)

Fix yy. Then

ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y)>r^​(y′)∣y)=ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y′)<r^​(y))=Fr^​(r^​(y)−),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\mid y\right)=\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})<\widehat{r}(y)\right)=F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-}), (84)

and

ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y)=r^​(y′)∣y)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\mid y\right) =ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y′)≤r^​(y))−ℙy′∼πref​(r^​(y′)<r^​(y))\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\leq\widehat{r}(y)\right)-\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})<\widehat{r}(y)\right) (85)
=Fr^​(r^​(y))−Fr^​(r^​(y)−).\displaystyle=F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))-F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-}). (86)

Plugging these two identities into the previous display yields (81).

Next, let V∼Unif⁡[0,1]V\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] be independent. By (82) and 𝔼⁡[V]=12\mathbb{E}[V]=\tfrac{1}{2},

𝔼​[u~​(y)∣y]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\tilde{u}(y)\mid y\big] =Fr^​(r^​(y)−)+𝔼⁡[V]⋅(Fr^​(r^​(y))−Fr^​(r^​(y)−))\displaystyle=F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\;+\;\mathbb{E}[V]\cdot\left(F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))-F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\right) (87)
=Fr^​(r^​(y)−)+12⋅(Fr^​(r^​(y))−Fr^​(r^​(y)−)).\displaystyle=F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))-F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\right). (88)

Taking 𝔼y∼π\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi} on both sides and comparing to (81) gives Rr^​(π)=𝔼y∼π,V​[u~​(y)]R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi,\;V}[\tilde{u}(y)].

Finally, we prove u~​(y′)∼Unif⁡[0,1]\tilde{u}(y^{\prime})\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] when y′∼πrefy^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. Let X:=r^​(y′)X:=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}) and write

A:=Fr^​(X−),B:=Fr^​(X),\displaystyle A:=F_{\widehat{r}}(X^{-}),\qquad B:=F_{\widehat{r}}(X), (89)

so that conditional on XX, u~​(y′)=A+V⁡(B−A)\tilde{u}(y^{\prime})=A+V(B-A) is uniform on the interval [A,B][A,B]. Fix any u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] and define the generalized inverse

tu:=inf{t∈ℝ:Fr^​(t)≥u}.\displaystyle t_{u}\;:=\;\inf\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\;F_{\widehat{r}}(t)\geq u\}. (90)

By definition of tut_{u}, we have Fr^​(tu−)≤u≤Fr^​(tu)F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})\leq u\leq F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}) and

ℙ⁡(X<tu)=Fr^​(tu−),ℙ⁡(X=tu)=Fr^​(tu)−Fr^​(tu−).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X<t_{u})=F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-}),\qquad\mathbb{P}(X=t_{u})=F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u})-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-}). (91)

Now decompose according to XX:

  • •

    If X<tuX<t_{u}, then B=Fr^​(X)≤Fr^​(tu−)≤uB=F_{\widehat{r}}(X)\leq F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})\leq u, hence ℙ⁡(u~≤u∣X)=1\mathbb{P}(\tilde{u}\leq u\mid X)=1.

  • •

    If X>tuX>t_{u}, then A=Fr^​(X−)≥Fr^​(tu)≥uA=F_{\widehat{r}}(X^{-})\geq F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u})\geq u, hence ℙ⁡(u~≤u∣X)=0\mathbb{P}(\tilde{u}\leq u\mid X)=0.

  • •

    If X=tuX=t_{u}, then by construction, u~\tilde{u} is uniform on [Fr^​(tu−),Fr^​(tu)][F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-}),F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u})], so

    ℙ⁡(u~≤u∣X=tu)=u−Fr^​(tu−)Fr^​(tu)−Fr^​(tu−).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\tilde{u}\leq u\mid X=t_{u})=\frac{u-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})}{F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u})-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})}. (92)

Therefore,

ℙ⁡(u~≤u)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\tilde{u}\leq u) =ℙ⁡(X<tu)⋅1+ℙ⁡(X=tu)⋅u−Fr^​(tu−)Fr^​(tu)−Fr^​(tu−)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(X<t_{u})\cdot 1\;+\;\mathbb{P}(X=t_{u})\cdot\frac{u-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})}{F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u})-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})} (93)
=Fr^​(tu−)+(Fr^​(tu)−Fr^​(tu−))⋅u−Fr^​(tu−)Fr^​(tu)−Fr^​(tu−)=u.\displaystyle=F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})\;+\;\left(F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u})-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})\right)\cdot\frac{u-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})}{F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u})-F_{\widehat{r}}(t_{u}^{-})}\;=\;u. (94)

Since this holds for all u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1], we conclude u~​(y′)∼Unif⁡[0,1]\tilde{u}(y^{\prime})\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1]. ∎

Appendix C Proofs for Best-of-NN

This section gives proofs for the guarantees of Best-of-NN in Section 3. The results in this section build on the guarantees for approximate rejection sampling as mentioned in Section 5.1, and are organized as follows:

  1. 1.

    Section C.1 provides a general upper bound on the regret of BoN in terms of the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence introduced in Section 2.3, and in Section C.2 we give a general lower bound on regret.

  2. 2.

    In Section C.3 we provide a lower bound to demonstrate the computational efficiency of BoN.

The proof of Theorem 3 below makes use of the approximate rejection sampling analysis of Block and Polyanskiy [2]. We briefly remind the reader that, given a base distribution πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and a target policy π≪πref\pi\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} with density ratio w:=d​π/d​πrefw:=d\pi/d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, classical rejection sampling draws y∼πrefy\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and accepts it with probability min⁡{w⁡(y)/M,1}\min\{w(y)/M,1\}; if w≤Mw\leq M πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s., then the accepted sample is exactly distributed as π\pi (Von Neumann [32]). When ww is not uniformly bounded, the same accept/reject rule truncates the target: mass in regions where w⁡(y)>Mw(y)>M cannot be fully realized and is effectively “clipped” at level MM. Running this procedure for NN proposals (returning a default proposal if no acceptance occurs) and MM sufficiently large induces a policy πR\pi_{R} that approximates π\pi in total variation, with error controlled by the clipped mass ℰM(π∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) plus an exponentially small failure-to-accept term (2; see Lemma 8).

C.1 Proof of Theorem 3

Proof.

As detailed in Section 5.1, in order to compare π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} to an arbitrary comparator π⋆\pi^{\star} under the true reward r⋆r^{\star}, we need to balance two competing effects: if NN is too small, BoN may fail to find responses comparable to those favored by π⋆\pi^{\star}; if NN is too large, BoN may overfit to r^\widehat{r} and pick outputs where r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} disagree. These two effects correspond exactly to the two terms in the upper bound (8), and they appear via the following regret decomposition, which holds for any M>0M>0: the regret Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^BoN)R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}) is equal to the sum of three terms,

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)⏟(T1)+Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)⏟(T2)+Rr^​(π^BoN)−Rr⋆​(π^BoN)⏟(T3),\displaystyle\underbrace{R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})}_{\mathrm{(T1)}}+\underbrace{R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})}_{\mathrm{(T2)}}+\underbrace{R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})}_{\mathrm{(T3)}}, (95)

where πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} is an intermediate comparator policy that is a closest MM-capped approximation to π⋆\pi^{\star} in total variation:

πM⋆∈argminπ≪πref:d​πd​πref≤M​πref​-a.s.TV(π⋆,π).\displaystyle\pi^{\star}_{M}\;\in\;\argmin_{\pi\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}:\;\frac{d\pi}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\leq M\ \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\text{-a.s.}}\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star},\pi). (96)

To bound (T1)\mathrm{(T1)}, we can further decompose

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M}) =Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(πM⋆)+Rr⋆​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)\displaystyle=R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})+R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M}) (97)

and control each of the two resulting terms separately. For the first difference, we observe that win-rate is bounded and thus 11-Lipschitz in total variation distance (it can be written as an expectation of the mid-CDF F~r^​(r^​(y))∈[0,1]\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))\in[0,1] as in Lemma 5), so we can control the loss from π⋆\pi^{\star} to πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} in terms of ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) by Block and Polyanskiy [2]: Lemma 6 shows that no policy with bounded density ratio can achieve total variation distance to π⋆\pi^{\star} less than ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) itself, and Lemma 7 demonstrates that the total variation distance between π⋆\pi^{\star} and πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} as defined above is less than ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), so TV(π⋆,πM⋆)=ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star},\pi^{\star}_{M})=\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), and hence

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(πM⋆)≤TV(π⋆,πM⋆)=ℰM(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\;\leq\;\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star},\pi^{\star}_{M})=\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (98)

For the second difference, we use the fact that the likelihood ratio of πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is upper bounded by MM almost surely to control the pairwise win rate error under πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} between r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star}. Specifically, we have wπM⋆​(y)≤Mw_{\pi^{\star}_{M}}(y)\leq M πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s., hence ℰM(πM⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}_{M}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0 and applying Lemma 4 with π=πM⋆\pi=\pi^{\star}_{M} and truncation MM yields

Rr⋆(πM⋆)−Rr^(πM⋆)≤Mεpw+ℰM(πM⋆∥πref)=Mεpw.\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\leq M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}_{M}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}. (99)

Putting these together, we have

(T1)=Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr^(πM⋆)≤ℰM(π⋆∥πref)+Mεpw.\displaystyle\mathrm{(T1)}=R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\leq\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}. (100)

To bound (T2)\mathrm{(T2)}, we introduce another intermediate comparator in order to utilize the optimality of π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} under r^\widehat{r} on a fixed batch of NN i.i.d. samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. Adopting the formalism of approximate rejection sampling from Block and Polyanskiy [2], we define a selection rule to be a policy πM,rej⋆\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}} that approximates πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} using only NN i.i.d. draws from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}; it returns the first accepted yiy_{i}, and if no acceptance occurs it returns y1y_{1}. We again further decompose (T2)\mathrm{(T2)} as

Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)=Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM,rej⋆)+Rr^​(πM,rej⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})=R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}})+R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}) (101)

and control each of the two resulting terms separately. For the first difference, we use the approximate rejection sampling analysis of Block and Polyanskiy [2] to show that πM,rej⋆\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}} approximates πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} in total variation distance up to an exponentially small term in N/MN/M, which again transfers to win-rate by boundedness. Thus

Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM,rej⋆)\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}}) ≤TV⁡(πM⋆,πM,rej⋆)\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{TV}\left(\pi^{\star}_{M},\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}}\right) (102)
≤ℰM(πM⋆∥πref)+12exp(−NM(1−ℰM(πM⋆∥πref)))\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}_{M}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+\frac{1}{2}\exp\left(-\frac{N}{M}\left(1-\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}_{M}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\right)\right) (103)
=12exp(−N/M),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\exp(-N/M), (104)

where the second inequality follows from Lemma 8, and the last equality holds because πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} is MM-capped, so ℰM(πM⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}_{M}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0. To bound the second difference, we observe that conditional on any fixed batch of NN samples from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, BoN simply selects the output with the highest r^\widehat{r} value, and thus dominates any other selection rule on that same batch under r^\widehat{r}, including πM,rej⋆\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}}. To make this concrete, we first apply Lemma 5 to rewrite win-rate under r^\widehat{r} as an expectation of F~r^​(r^​(⋅))\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(\cdot)), so that

Rr^​(πM,rej⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}) =𝔼y∼πM,rej⋆​[F~r^​(r^​(y))]−𝔼y∼π^BoN​[F~r^​(r^​(y))].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}}}\!\left[\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}\!\left(\widehat{r}(y)\right)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}}\!\left[\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}\!\left(\widehat{r}(y)\right)\right]. (105)

We can now appeal to the optimality of π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} under r^\widehat{r}. Below, we use 𝔼𝒴^N∼πref​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[\cdot] to refer to expectations over NN samples 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N} drawn from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, and, given 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}, we use 𝔼πM,rej⋆|𝒴^N​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}}\mid\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}}[\cdot] to refer to the expectation over responses induced by running approximate rejection sampling conditioned on the realization of the set 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N} drawn by the algorithm; we define 𝔼π^BoN|𝒴^N​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}\mid\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}}[\cdot] analogously. We can then use the linearity of expectation, so that

𝔼𝒴^N∼πref​[𝔼y∼πM,rej⋆|𝒴^N​[F~r^​(r^​(y))]−𝔼y∼π^BoN|𝒴^N​[F~r^​(r^​(y))]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}}\mid\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}}\!\left[\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)\right)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}\mid\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}}\!\left[\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)\right)\right]\right] (106)

couples the set 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N} drawn by the two algorithms, and compares the performance of π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} and πM,rej⋆\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}} for a fixed set of NN responses. Then, because the BoN policy always chooses a response with the largest value under r^\widehat{r} for any fixed 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}, and F~r^\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}} is nondecreasing, we have F~r^​(r^​(y))≤maxi∈[N]⁡F~r^​(r^​(yi))\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))\leq\max_{i\in[N]}\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y_{i})) for all y∈𝒴^Ny\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}. Therefore,

Rr^​(πM,rej⋆)−Rr^​(π^BoN)≤0.\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M,\mathrm{rej}})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})\leq 0. (107)

Combining these steps gives

(T2)=Rr^(πM⋆)−Rr^(π^BoN)≤12exp(−N/M).\displaystyle\mathrm{(T2)}=R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})\leq\frac{1}{2}\exp(-N/M). (108)

Finally, we control (T3)\mathrm{(T3)} using a similar change-of-measure argument as for (T1)\mathrm{(T1)}. Before applying Lemma 4 again, we first show that BoN has density ratio at most NN relative to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, and thus the pairwise win-rate error under π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} between r^\widehat{r} and r⋆r^{\star} is at most N⋅εpw​(r^)N\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}). Let 𝒴^N:=(y1,…,yN)∈𝒴N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}:=(y_{1},\dots,y_{N})\in\mathcal{Y}^{N} denote the sequence of NN i.i.d. draws from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, and write

πref​(𝒴^N):=∏i=1Nπref​(yi)\displaystyle\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N})\;:=\;\prod_{i=1}^{N}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{i}) (109)

Since conditioned on 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}, the BoN algorithm outputs a single element of 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N} deterministically (via the fixed tie-breaking rule), we can write π^BoN\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} in closed form as

π^BoN(y)=∑𝒴^N∈𝒴Nπref(𝒴^N)⋅𝟏{y∈𝒴^N}⋅𝟏{r^(y)≥r^(y′)∀y′∈𝒴^N}.\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}(y)\;=\;\sum_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\in\mathcal{Y}^{N}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N})\cdot\mathbf{1}\{y\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\}\cdot\mathbf{1}\Big\{\widehat{r}(y)\geq\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\ \ \forall\,y^{\prime}\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\Big\}. (110)

Next, express πref​(y)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y) by marginalizing over 𝒴^N\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N} and then sampling an index uniformly from {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\}:

πref​(y)=∑𝒴^N∈𝒴Nπref​(𝒴^N)⋅∑y′∈𝒴^N𝟏{y′=y}N.\displaystyle\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)\;=\;\sum_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\in\mathcal{Y}^{N}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N})\cdot\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}}\frac{\mathbf{1}\{y^{\prime}=y\}}{N}. (111)

Combining (110) and (111), for any yy with πref​(y)>0\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)>0 we have

π^BoN​(y)πref​(y)\displaystyle\frac{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}(y)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)} =N⋅∑𝒴^N∈𝒴Nπref(𝒴^N)⋅𝟏{y∈𝒴^N}⋅𝟏{r^(y)≥r^(y′)∀y′∈𝒴^N}∑𝒴^N∈𝒴Nπref(𝒴^N)⋅∑y′∈𝒴^N𝟏{y′=y}\displaystyle=N\cdot\frac{\sum_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\in\mathcal{Y}^{N}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N})\cdot\mathbf{1}\{y\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\}\cdot\mathbf{1}\Big\{\widehat{r}(y)\geq\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\ \forall\,y^{\prime}\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\Big\}}{\sum_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\in\mathcal{Y}^{N}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N})\cdot\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}}\mathbf{1}\{y^{\prime}=y\}} (112)
≤N⋅∑𝒴^N∈𝒴Nπref(𝒴^N)⋅𝟏{y∈𝒴^N}∑𝒴^N∈𝒴Nπref(𝒴^N)⋅𝟏{y∈𝒴^N}\displaystyle\leq N\cdot\frac{\sum_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\in\mathcal{Y}^{N}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N})\cdot\mathbf{1}\{y\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\}}{\sum_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\in\mathcal{Y}^{N}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N})\cdot\mathbf{1}\{y\in\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\}} (113)
=N.\displaystyle=N. (114)

Thus π^BoN/πref≤N\nicefrac{{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}}}{{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}\leq N pointwise, and by definition,

ℰN(π^BoN∥πref)=𝔼y∼πref[(π^BoN​(y)πref​(y)−N)+]=0.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{N}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[\Big(\frac{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}(y)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)}-N\Big)_{+}\right]=0. (115)

Now we can apply Lemma 4 to π=π^BoN\pi=\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} with truncation M=NM=N such that

(T3)≤Nεpw+ℰN(π^BoN∥πref)=Nεpw.\displaystyle\mathrm{(T3)}\leq N\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}+\mathcal{E}_{N}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=N\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}. (116)

Combining all the preceding bounds, we obtain

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(π^BoN)≲ℰM(π⋆∥πref)+(M+N)εpw+exp(−N/M).\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}})\lesssim\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+(M+N)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}+\exp(-N/M). (117)

Setting M=N/log⁡(1/εpw​(r^))M=N/\log\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})}}\right) and observing that for such MM, it holds that exp(−N/M)=εpw(r^)\exp(-N/M)=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}), we obtain the desired result. ∎

Lemma 6 (Lemma 32 in Block and Polyanskiy [2]).

Fix N≥1N\geq 1 and assume π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} with density ratio w⋆:=d​π⋆/d​πrefw^{\star}:=\nicefrac{{d\pi^{\star}}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}. Then for any π≪πref\pi\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} whose density ratio w:=d​π/d​πrefw:=\nicefrac{{d\pi}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}} satisfies w≤Mw\leq M πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s., we have

TV(π,π⋆)≥ℰM(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle\mathrm{TV}(\pi,\pi^{\star})\;\geq\;\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (118)
Lemma 7.

Fix N≥1N\geq 1 and assume π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} with density ratio w⋆:=d​π⋆/d​πrefw^{\star}:=\nicefrac{{d\pi^{\star}}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}. Then there exists a policy πM⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}_{M}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} such that d​πM⋆d​πref​(y)≤Mπref\frac{d\pi^{\star}_{M}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)\leq M\ \ \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s., and

TV(πM⋆,π⋆)=ℰM(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star}_{M},\pi^{\star})=\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (119)
Proof.

Define the clipped density

wM​(y):=min⁡{w⋆​(y),M}.\displaystyle w_{M}(y)\;:=\;\min\{w^{\star}(y),\,M\}. (120)

Using w⋆=wM+(w⋆−M)+w^{\star}=w_{M}+(w^{\star}-M)_{+} pointwise and 𝔼y∼πref​[w⋆​(y)]=1\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w^{\star}(y)]=1, we get

𝔼y∼πref[wM(y)]= 1−ℰM(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w_{M}(y)]\;=\;1-\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (121)

Thus wMw_{M} has total mass 1−ℰM(π⋆∥πref)1-\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) but is not yet a valid probability density when ℰM(π⋆∥πref)>0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})>0, so we must add back the excess mass while ensuring that the density ratio is still bounded. Define the slack under MM:

S:=𝔼y∼πref​[(M−w⋆​(y))+].\displaystyle S\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big[(M-w^{\star}(y))_{+}\big]. (122)

Since (M−w⋆)+=M−min⁡{w⋆,M}=M−wM(M-w^{\star})_{+}=M-\min\{w^{\star},M\}=M-w_{M} pointwise, we have

S=M−𝔼y∼πref[wM(y)]=M−(1−ℰM(π⋆∥πref))≥ℰM(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle S=M-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w_{M}(y)]=M-(1-\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}))\geq\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (123)

If ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0, we set g≡0g\equiv 0 and πM⋆=π⋆\pi^{\star}_{M}=\pi^{\star} and we are done. Otherwise we define

g(y):=ℰM(π⋆∥πref)⋅(M−w⋆​(y))+S.\displaystyle g(y)\;:=\;\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\cdot\frac{(M-w^{\star}(y))_{+}}{S}. (124)

Then 0≤g⁡(y)≤(M−w⋆​(y))+0\leq g(y)\leq(M-w^{\star}(y))_{+} πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s. and 𝔼y∼πref[g(y)]=ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[g(y)]=\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). Now we define πM⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}_{M}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} via

d​πM⋆d​πref​(y):=wM​(y)+g⁡(y).\displaystyle\frac{d\pi^{\star}_{M}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)\;:=\;w_{M}(y)+g(y). (125)

We can verify that normalization holds:

𝔼y∼πref[d​πM⋆d​πref(y)]=𝔼y∼πref[wM(y)]+𝔼y∼πref[g(y)]=(1−ℰM(π⋆∥πref))+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=1.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[\frac{d\pi^{\star}_{M}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w_{M}(y)]+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[g(y)]=(1-\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}))+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=1. (126)

In addition, the pointwise density ratio bound still holds: if w⋆​(y)>Mw^{\star}(y)>M then wM​(y)=Mw_{M}(y)=M and (M−w⋆​(y))+=0(M-w^{\star}(y))_{+}=0, so g⁡(y)=0g(y)=0 and wM​(y)+g⁡(y)=Mw_{M}(y)+g(y)=M; if w⋆​(y)≤Mw^{\star}(y)\leq M then wM​(y)=w⋆​(y)w_{M}(y)=w^{\star}(y) and g⁡(y)≤M−w⋆​(y)g(y)\leq M-w^{\star}(y), so wM​(y)+g⁡(y)≤Mw_{M}(y)+g(y)\leq M. Hence ℰM(πM⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}_{M}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0. Finally, we compute the total variation distance using densities:

TV⁡(π⋆,πM⋆)=12​𝔼y∼πref​[|w⋆​(y)−(wM​(y)+g⁡(y))|].\displaystyle\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star},\pi^{\star}_{M})=\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[\Big|w^{\star}(y)-\big(w_{M}(y)+g(y)\big)\Big|\right]. (127)

Pointwise,

|w⋆​(y)−(wM​(y)+g⁡(y))|=(w⋆​(y)−M)++g⁡(y),\displaystyle\Big|w^{\star}(y)-\big(w_{M}(y)+g(y)\big)\Big|=(w^{\star}(y)-M)_{+}+g(y), (128)

because on {w⋆>M}\{w^{\star}>M\} we have wM=Mw_{M}=M and g=0g=0, while on {w⋆≤M}\{w^{\star}\leq M\} we have wM=w⋆w_{M}=w^{\star}. Taking expectations gives

𝔼y∼πref​[|w⋆​(y)−(wM​(y)+g⁡(y))|]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[\Big|w^{\star}(y)-\big(w_{M}(y)+g(y)\big)\Big|\right] =𝔼y∼πref​[(w⋆​(y)−M)+]+𝔼y∼πref​[g⁡(y)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[(w^{\star}(y)-M)_{+}]+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[g(y)] (129)
=2ℰM(π⋆∥πref),\displaystyle=2\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), (130)

hence TV(π⋆,πM⋆)=ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star},\pi^{\star}_{M})=\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), which implies the stated upper bound. ∎

The following lemma (which is originally adapted from Theorem 3 in Block and Polyanskiy [2]) contains sample complexity upper bounds for the approximate rejection sampling procedure detailed in Block and Polyanskiy [2]. We refer to Huang et al. [14] for a detailed discussion of this result.

Lemma 8 (Lemma D.4 in Huang et al. [14]).

For any valid policy π∈Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal{Y}), and N,M>0N,M>0, let πR∈Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi_{R}\in\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) be the law of responses induced by running approximate rejection sampling. Then

TV(π,πR)≤ℰM(π∥πref)+12exp(−N⋅(1−ℰM(π∥πref)M).\displaystyle\mathrm{TV}(\pi,\pi_{R})\leq\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+\frac{1}{2}\exp\left(-\frac{N\cdot(1-\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})}{M}\right). (131)

C.2 Proof of Theorem 4

We first restate the theorem for the sake of completeness, after which we provide the proof.

Theorem 8.

For any non-atomic πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, any π^𝒜\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{A}} in the sample-and-evaluate framework, and any ε<1/2\varepsilon<\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}, there exist reward functions r^\widehat{r}, r⋆r^{\star} satisfying εpw​(r^)≤ε\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\leq\varepsilon and a comparator policy π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} for which

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(π^𝒜)≥k⋅infM≥1{M⋅ε+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)},\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{A}})\geq k\cdot\inf_{M\geq 1}\left\{M\cdot\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\right\}, (132)

for some universal constant k>0k>0.

Proof.

We build a hard instance in three steps. First, we identify a large-probability region SS on which π^\widehat{\pi} cannot overweight πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} by more than a constant factor; inside SS we carve out a small set AA whose πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-mass is on the order of the pairwise-error budget ε\varepsilon where π^​(A)≲ε\widehat{\pi}(A)\lesssim\varepsilon. Next, we choose a simple reward pair (r^,r⋆)(\widehat{r},r^{\star}) so that the algorithm cannot reliably distinguish AA from AcA^{c} while still meeting the pairwise-error budget. Then, we let π⋆\pi^{\star} upweight πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} by a factor of M⋆M^{\star} on AA, which forces π⋆​(A)≈M⋆​ε\pi^{\star}(A)\approx M^{\star}\varepsilon. Since the regret is proportional to π⋆​(A)−π^​(A)\pi^{\star}(A)-\widehat{\pi}(A) in our instance, we will relate this regret to the skyline objective.

First, we construct a small set AA on which π^\widehat{\pi} has small mass. Fix any sample-and-evaluate algorithm π^\widehat{\pi}. Let w^​(y):=d​π^/d​πref​(y)\hat{w}(y):=\nicefrac{{d\widehat{\pi}}}{{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}(y) so that 𝔼πref​[w^]=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[\hat{w}]=1. By Markov’s inequality,

ℙy∼πref​(w^​(y)>2)≤12,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\hat{w}(y)>2\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}, (133)

so S:={w^≤2}S:=\{\hat{w}\leq 2\} satisfies πref​(S)≥12\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(S)\geq\frac{1}{2}. Set

ε′:=min⁡{ε, 1/M⋆}∈(0,12].\displaystyle\varepsilon^{\prime}:=\min\{\varepsilon,\,1/M^{\star}\}\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}]. (134)

Since πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is non-atomic and ε′≤πref​(S)\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(S), choose a measurable A⊆SA\subseteq S with πref​(A)=ε′\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)=\varepsilon^{\prime}. Then

π^​(A)=∫Aw^​d​πref≤2​πref​(A)=2​ε′.\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}(A)=\int_{A}\hat{w}\,d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\leq 2\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)=2\varepsilon^{\prime}. (135)

We set ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} in this way for two reasons: first, the comparator we construct below will place density M⋆M^{\star} on AA, so feasibility requires π⋆​(A)=M⋆​πref​(A)≤1\pi^{\star}(A)=M^{\star}\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)\leq 1, i.e. πref​(A)≤1/M⋆\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)\leq 1/M^{\star}. In addition, we will enforce the pairwise-error budget by choosing πref​(A)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A) no larger than ε\varepsilon under the pairwise error, as we will see next. Define

r⋆(y):=𝟏{y∈A},r^(y)≡0.\displaystyle r^{\star}(y):=\mathbf{1}\{y\in A\},\qquad\widehat{r}(y)\equiv 0. (136)

Intuitively, r⋆r^{\star} makes AA the uniquely desirable region, while a constant r^\widehat{r} provides no signal about membership in AA, so any reliable preference for AA must come from chance rather than information. For any reward function rr, recall the pairwise outcome

ϕr(y,y′)=𝟏{r(y)>r(y′)}+12 1{r(y)=r(y′)},\displaystyle\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime})=\mathbf{1}\{r(y)>r(y^{\prime})\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{r(y)=r(y^{\prime})\}, (137)

and the pairwise error

εpw​(r^)=𝔼y,y′∼πref​[|ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−ϕr^​(y,y′)|].\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})=\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\,\left|\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})\right|\,\right]. (138)

Since r^\widehat{r} is constant, ϕr^​(y,y′)≡12\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})\equiv\tfrac{1}{2}. Under r⋆=𝟏Ar^{\star}=\mathbf{1}_{A}, we have ϕr⋆​(y,y′)∈{0,12,1}\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{2},1\} and |ϕr⋆​(y,y′)−12|=12\left|\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})-\tfrac{1}{2}\right|=\tfrac{1}{2} iff exactly one of (y,y′)(y,y^{\prime}) lies in AA. Thus

εpw​(r^)=12⋅ℙy,y′∼πref​(𝟏A​(y)≠𝟏A​(y′))=12⋅2​ε′​(1−ε′)≤ε′≤ε.\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\mathbf{1}_{A}(y)\neq\mathbf{1}_{A}(y^{\prime})\right)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\varepsilon^{\prime}(1-\varepsilon^{\prime})\leq\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq\varepsilon. (139)

Next, we construct π⋆\pi^{\star} and evaluate the skyline objective. Define π⋆≪πref\pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} via

w⋆​(y):=d​π⋆d​πref​(y)={M⋆,y∈A,c,y∉A,c:=1−M⋆​ε′1−ε′≥0(since ​ε′≤1/M⋆).\displaystyle w^{\star}(y):=\frac{d\pi^{\star}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)=\begin{cases}M^{\star},&y\in A,\\ c,&y\notin A,\end{cases}\qquad c:=\frac{1-M^{\star}\varepsilon^{\prime}}{1-\varepsilon^{\prime}}\geq 0\quad(\text{since }\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq 1/M^{\star}). (140)

Note that since M⋆≥1M^{\star}\geq 1 and ε′∈(0,1)\varepsilon^{\prime}\in(0,1), we have 1−M⋆​ε′≤1−ε′1-M^{\star}\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq 1-\varepsilon^{\prime}, hence c≤1c\leq 1. Then 𝔼πref​[w⋆]=M⋆​ε′+c⁡(1−ε′)=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w^{\star}]=M^{\star}\varepsilon^{\prime}+c(1-\varepsilon^{\prime})=1, so π⋆\pi^{\star} is a valid policy and

π⋆​(A)=∫Aw⋆​d​πref=M⋆​ε′.\displaystyle\pi^{\star}(A)=\int_{A}w^{\star}\,d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=M^{\star}\varepsilon^{\prime}. (141)

Moreover, for any M∈[c,M⋆]M\in[c,M^{\star}],

ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=𝔼πref[(w⋆−M)+]=(M⋆−M)πref(A)=(M⋆−M)ε′.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[(w^{\star}-M)_{+}\right]=(M^{\star}-M)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)=(M^{\star}-M)\varepsilon^{\prime}. (142)

Hence for such MM,

Mε+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=Mε+(M⋆−M)ε′=M⋆ε′+M(ε−ε′).\displaystyle M\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=M\varepsilon+(M^{\star}-M)\varepsilon^{\prime}=M^{\star}\varepsilon^{\prime}+M(\varepsilon-\varepsilon^{\prime}). (143)

Next, we can explicitly compute the win-rate and regret. Fix any policy π\pi and write πref​(A)=ε′\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)=\varepsilon^{\prime}. Using the definition of win-rate under r⋆=𝟏Ar^{\star}=\mathbf{1}_{A}:

Rr⋆​(π)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi) =ℙ⁡(r⋆​(y)>r⋆​(y′))+12​ℙ​(r⋆​(y)=r⋆​(y′))\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(r^{\star}(y)>r^{\star}(y^{\prime}))+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}(r^{\star}(y)=r^{\star}(y^{\prime})) (144)
=π⁡(A)​(1−πref​(A))+12​(π⁡(A)​πref​(A)+(1−π⁡(A))​(1−πref​(A)))\displaystyle=\pi(A)(1-\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A))+\frac{1}{2}\left(\pi(A)\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A)+(1-\pi(A))(1-\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A))\right) (145)
=12​(1−πref​(A))+12​π​(A).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(1-\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A))+\frac{1}{2}\,\pi(A). (146)

Subtracting for π=π⋆\pi=\pi^{\star} and π=π^\pi=\widehat{\pi} cancels the tie-mass term, yielding

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^)=12​(π⋆​(A)−π^​(A)).\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\pi^{\star}(A)-\widehat{\pi}(A)\right). (147)

Combining (147) with (141) and (135) gives

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^)≥12​(M⋆​ε′−2​ε′)=M⋆−22​ε′.\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi})\geq\frac{1}{2}\left(M^{\star}\varepsilon^{\prime}-2\varepsilon^{\prime}\right)=\frac{M^{\star}-2}{2}\,\varepsilon^{\prime}. (148)

Finally, we relate the regret to the skyline objective. We consider two regimes.

Case 1: M⋆​ε≤1M^{\star}\varepsilon\leq 1. Then ε′=ε\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon, and (143) gives, for all M∈[c,M⋆]M\in[c,M^{\star}],

Mε+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=M⋆ε.\displaystyle M\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=M^{\star}\varepsilon. (149)

In particular,

infM≥1{Mε+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)}=M⋆ε.\displaystyle\inf_{M\geq 1}\{M\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\}=M^{\star}\varepsilon. (150)

Indeed, for M>M⋆M>M^{\star}, ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0 so M​ε≥M⋆​εM\varepsilon\geq M^{\star}\varepsilon; thus the infimum over M≥1M\geq 1 equals M⋆​εM^{\star}\varepsilon. Combining with (148), for M⋆≥4M^{\star}\geq 4,

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr⋆(π^)≥M⋆−22ε≥14M⋆ε=14infM≥1{Mε+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)}.\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi})\geq\frac{M^{\star}-2}{2}\,\varepsilon\geq\frac{1}{4}\,M^{\star}\varepsilon=\frac{1}{4}\inf_{M\geq 1}\{M\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\}. (151)

Case 2: M⋆​ε>1M^{\star}\varepsilon>1. Then ε′=1/M⋆\varepsilon^{\prime}=1/M^{\star}, so (148) yields

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^)≥M⋆−22​M⋆≥14,\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi})\geq\frac{M^{\star}-2}{2M^{\star}}\geq\frac{1}{4}, (152)

with M⋆≥4M^{\star}\geq 4. On the other hand, for any M≥1M\geq 1, we have ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=𝔼πref[(w⋆−M)+]≤𝔼πref[w⋆]=1\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[(w^{\star}-M)_{+}]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w^{\star}]=1, so using ε≤12\varepsilon\leq\tfrac{1}{2},

infM≥1{Mε+ℰM(π⋆∥πref)}≤ε+1≤32.\displaystyle\inf_{M\geq 1}\{M\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\}\leq\varepsilon+1\leq\frac{3}{2}. (153)

C.3 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

Fix M≥2M\geq 2. We construct a hard instance in which the optimal policy must place all its weight on a subset of πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, and show that any algorithm in the sample-and-evaluate framework requires on the order of MM samples to sample from this subset and avoid suffering constant regret. Let 𝒴=[0,1]\mathcal{Y}=[0,1] and let πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} be Unif⁡[0,1]\mathrm{Unif}[0,1]. Define

I:=[1−1M, 1],πref​(I)=1M.I:=\left[1-\frac{1}{M},\,1\right],\qquad\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(I)=\frac{1}{M}. (154)

Set r^(y)=r⋆(y):=𝟏{y∈I}\hat{r}(y)=r^{\star}(y):=\mathbf{1}\{y\in I\}, so εpw​(r^,r⋆)=0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\hat{r},r^{\star})=0. Let π⋆:=πref(⋅∣I)\pi^{\star}:=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid I) so that d​π⋆d​πref(y)=M𝟏{y∈I}\frac{d\pi^{\star}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)=M\mathbf{1}\{y\in I\} and hence ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0. Moreover, r⋆​(y)=1r^{\star}(y)=1 a.s. under π⋆\pi^{\star}, and r⋆​(y′)=1r^{\star}(y^{\prime})=1 w.p. 1/M1/M under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, so

Rr⋆​(π⋆)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star}) =ℙy∼π⋆,y′∼πref​(r⋆​(y)>r⋆​(y′))+12⋅ℙy∼π⋆,y′∼πref​(r⋆​(y)=r⋆​(y′))\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi^{\star},y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left(r^{\star}(y)>r^{\star}(y^{\prime})\right)+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi^{\star},y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left(r^{\star}(y)=r^{\star}(y^{\prime})\right) (155)
=(1−1M)+12⋅1M\displaystyle=\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{M} (156)
=1−12​M.\displaystyle=1-\frac{1}{2M}. (157)

Let y1,…,yN​∼iid​πrefy_{1},\dots,y_{N}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} be the samples and let y^\hat{y} be 𝒜\mathcal{A}’s output. By the sample-and-evaluate framework, y^∈{y1,…,yN}\hat{y}\in\{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\} almost surely. In addition, define the event E:={∃i∈[N]:yi∈I}E:=\{\exists i\in[N]:y_{i}\in I\}. On EcE^{c} we have yi∉Iy_{i}\notin I for all ii, hence r⋆​(y^)=0r^{\star}(\hat{y})=0 deterministically and therefore

Rr⋆​(π𝒜∣Ec)=12⋅ℙy′∼πref​(r⋆​(y′)=0)=12​(1−1M)=12−12​M.R^{r^{\star}}(\pi_{\mathcal{A}}\mid E^{c})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(r^{\star}(y^{\prime})=0\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right)=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2M}. (158)

Using (155), on EcE^{c} we obtain

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π𝒜∣Ec)=12.R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\pi_{\mathcal{A}}\mid E^{c})=\frac{1}{2}. (159)

Since regret is nonnegative, taking expectations yields

𝔼⁡[Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π𝒜)]≥ℙ⁡(Ec)⋅12=12​(1−1M)N.\mathbb{E}\left[R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\pi_{\mathcal{A}})\right]\geq\mathbb{P}(E^{c})\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right)^{N}. (160)

If the expected regret is at most δ\delta, then the above implies

(1−1M)N≤2​δ.\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right)^{N}\leq 2\delta. (161)

When δ<12\delta<\frac{1}{2}, the RHS is <1<1, so taking logs on both sides gives

N​log⁡(1−1M)≤log⁡(2​δ)⟹N≥log⁡(12​δ)log⁡(MM−1).\displaystyle N\log\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right)\leq\log(2\delta)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N\geq\frac{\log(\tfrac{1}{2\delta})}{\log(\tfrac{M}{M-1})}. (162)

For M≥2M\geq 2, we can apply x≤−log⁡(1−x)≤x1−xx\leq-\log(1-x)\leq\frac{x}{1-x} with x=1/Mx=1/M, yielding

N≳M​log⁡(1δ).\displaystyle N\gtrsim M\log\left(\tfrac{1}{\delta}\right). (163)

∎

Appendix D Proofs for Monotone Algorithms

This section gives proofs for the guarantees in Section 4, and are organized as follows:

  1. 1.

    Section D.1 provides a derivation of the optimal policy to the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized variation problem, which is introduced in Section 4.

  2. 2.

    Section D.2 provides a general upper bound on the regret of monotone algorithm in terms of the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence introduced in Section 2.3, matching the skyline lower bound on regret.

  3. 3.

    In Section D.3 we provide a separation result between ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized BoN and the only other provably monotone algorithm: the solution to the χ2\chi^{2}-regularized variational problem as analyzed in Huang et al. [14]. Importantly, this highlights the weaknesses of previous approaches under a win-rate regret goal.

D.1 Derivation of ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-Regularized BoN Policy

Throughout this section, we fix a measurable score function s:𝒴→[0,1]s:\mathcal{Y}\to[0,1] on a finite 𝒴\mathcal{Y}; similar arguments apply to any bounded score range and infinite response space. Consider the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized variational problem parameterized by β>0\beta>0:

maxπ≪πref{𝔼π[s(y)]−βℰM(π∥πref)}\displaystyle\max_{\pi\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\Big\{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[s(y)]-\beta\,\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\Big\} (164)

which is equivalently the functional optimization over ww:

maxw≥0,𝔼y∼πref​[w⁡(y)]=1⁡{𝔼πref​[w⁡(y)​s​(y)]−β​𝔼πref​[(w⁡(y)−M)+]}.\displaystyle\max_{w\geq 0,\ \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w(y)]=1}\ \Big\{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big[w(y)s(y)\big]-\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big[(w(y)-M)_{+}\big]\Big\}. (165)
Lemma 9.

Fix M≥2M\geq 2 and β≥1\beta\geq 1. Then there exists an optimizer w⋆w^{\star} to (165) satisfying 0≤w⋆​(y)≤M0\leq w^{\star}(y)\leq M πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s., and consequently ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0 at the optimum (where π⋆:=w⋆​πref\pi^{\star}:=w^{\star}\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). In particular, (165) is equivalent to

maxw: 0≤w≤M,𝔼y∼πref​[w⁡(y)]=1𝔼πref[w(y)s(y)],\displaystyle\max_{w:\ 0\leq w\leq M,\ \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w(y)]=1}\ \mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w(y)s(y)], (166)

or, returning to π\pi,

maxπ≪πref:d​π/d​πref≤M𝔼π[s].\displaystyle\max_{\pi\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}:\ d\pi/d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\leq M}\ \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[s]. (167)
Proof.

Define the primal objective

J⁡(w):=𝔼πref​[w⁡(y)​s​(y)]−β​𝔼πref​[(w⁡(y)−M)+],s.t. ​w≥0,𝔼πref​[w]=1.\displaystyle J(w)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big[w(y)s(y)\big]-\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big[(w(y)-M)_{+}\big],\qquad\text{s.t. }w\geq 0,\ \mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w]=1. (168)

Since 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is finite, this is a finite-dimensional convex program: the penalty term is concave, so JJ is concave in ww, and the constraints are affine. Slater’s condition holds because w≡1w\equiv 1 is strictly feasible (w⁡(y)>0w(y)>0 for all yy and 𝔼πref​[w]=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w]=1), so strong duality applies. Next, we introduce a scalar Lagrange multiplier α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} for the constraint 𝔼πref​[w]=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w]=1. The Lagrangian is

ℒ⁡(w,α)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(w,\alpha)\; =𝔼πref​[w⁡(y)​s​(y)−β​(w⁡(y)−M)+]−α⁡(𝔼πref​[w]−1)\displaystyle=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\big[w(y)s(y)-\beta(w(y)-M)_{+}\big]-\alpha\big(\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w]-1\big) (169)
=α+𝔼πref​[w⁡(y)​(s⁡(y)−α)−β​(w⁡(y)−M)+].\displaystyle=\;\alpha+\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\big[w(y)(s(y)-\alpha)-\beta(w(y)-M)_{+}\big]. (170)

For fixed α\alpha, the maximization over ww separates over yy: for each yy we maximize, over u≥0u\geq 0,

ϕy​(α):=maxu≥0⁡{u⁡(s⁡(y)−α)−β​(u−M)+}.\displaystyle\phi_{y}(\alpha)\;:=\;\max_{u\geq 0}\ \Big\{u\,(s(y)-\alpha)-\beta(u-M)_{+}\Big\}. (171)

This is a 1D piecewise-linear problem. Writing s=s⁡(y)s=s(y),

u⁡(s−α)−β​(u−M)+={u⁡(s−α),0≤u≤M,u⁡(s−α−β)+β​M,u≥M.\displaystyle u(s-\alpha)-\beta(u-M)_{+}=\begin{cases}u(s-\alpha),&0\leq u\leq M,\\ u(s-\alpha-\beta)+\beta M,&u\geq M.\end{cases} (172)

Hence:

  • •

    If s−α−β>0s-\alpha-\beta>0 for some yy, then ϕy​(α)=+∞\phi_{y}(\alpha)=+\infty (the u≥Mu\geq M branch has positive slope), so the dual function is infinite. Therefore any dual-optimal α⋆\alpha^{\star} must satisfy

    s⁡(y)−α⋆−β≤0for all ​y∈𝒴.\displaystyle s(y)-\alpha^{\star}-\beta\leq 0\quad\text{for all }y\in\mathcal{Y}. (173)
  • •

    Under this condition, the u≥Mu\geq M branch has nonpositive slope, so its maximizers can be chosen at u=Mu=M. Thus, for every yy, there exists a maximizer of ϕy​(α⋆)\phi_{y}(\alpha^{\star}) lying in [0,M][0,M]. In other words: for any α\alpha with finite dual value, the inner maximization can be restricted to 0≤u≤M0\leq u\leq M.

By strong duality, there exists a primal optimizer w⋆w^{\star} that attains the (finite) dual optimum at some α⋆\alpha^{\star}, and by the pointwise conclusion above we may choose w⋆​(y)∈[0,M]w^{\star}(y)\in[0,M] for every yy. For such a w⋆w^{\star}, we have (w⋆​(y)−M)+=0(w^{\star}(y)-M)_{+}=0 for all yy, hence ℰM(π⋆∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0 and

J⁡(w⋆)=𝔼πref​[w⋆​s].\displaystyle J(w^{\star})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w^{\star}s]. (174)

Therefore, the optimal value of (165) equals the optimal value of (166), i.e., we may restrict attention (without loss) to policies whose density ratios satisfy 0≤w≤M0\leq w\leq M πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s.; moreover, an optimizer exists within this restricted class. ∎

With this simplification in hand, we may work directly with the equivalent density-ratio program (166). Since the problem is convex and strong duality holds, we can characterize the optimizer by the KKT conditions, which are necessary and sufficient for optimality [3]. We now apply these conditions to derive the optimal policy. In the following proposition, we assume for the sake of simplicity that there exists a threshold α⋆\alpha^{\star} so that ℙy∼πref​(s⁡(y)≥α⋆)=1/M\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(s(y)\geq\alpha^{\star})=1/M exactly; otherwise one can randomize inclusion on the boundary set {y:s⁡(y)=α⋆}\{y:s(y)=\alpha^{\star}\} to make the selected πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-mass exactly 1/M1/M, without affecting optimality.

Proposition 4.

Consider (166) and assume the existence of an optimizer via Lemma 9. Fix M≥2M\geq 2. Then there exists a threshold α∗∈ℝ\alpha^{*}\in\mathbb{R} such that an optimal density ratio satisfies

w⋆(y)=M 1{s(y)≥α∗}(πref-a.s.),\displaystyle w^{\star}(y)=M\,\mathbf{1}\{s(y)\geq\alpha^{*}\}\qquad(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\text{-a.s.}), (175)

where α∗\alpha^{*} can be chosen so that ℙy∼πref​(s⁡(y)≥α⋆)=1/M\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(s(y)\geq\alpha^{\star})=1/M. Equivalently, the optimal policy is

πM(⋅)=πref(⋅∣s(⋅)≥α∗),\displaystyle\pi_{M}(\cdot)=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid s(\cdot)\geq\alpha^{*}), (176)

i.e., the top-1/M1/M score-threshold policy.

Proof.

We solve (166) via the Lagrangian/KKT conditions. Introduce a scalar multiplier α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} for the equality constraint 𝔼y∼πref​[w​(y)]=1\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w(y)]=1, and pointwise multipliers μ⁡(y)≥0\mu(y)\geq 0 and ν⁡(y)≥0\nu(y)\geq 0 for the inequality constraints w⁡(y)≥0w(y)\geq 0 and w⁡(y)≤Mw(y)\leq M, respectively. The Lagrangian is

ℒ⁡(w,α,μ,ν)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(w;\alpha,\mu,\nu) :=𝔼y∼πref​[w⁡(y)​s​(y)]−α⁡(𝔼y∼πref​[w⁡(y)]−1)\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w(y)\,s(y)]-\alpha\big(\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w(y)]-1\big) (177)
+𝔼y∼πref​[μ⁡(y)​w​(y)]+𝔼y∼πref​[ν⁡(y)​(M−w⁡(y))].\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[\mu(y)\,w(y)]+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[\nu(y)\,(M-w(y))]. (178)

The KKT conditions at an optimum (w⋆,α⋆,μ⋆,ν⋆)(w^{\star},\alpha^{\star},\mu^{\star},\nu^{\star}) are:

(i) Primal feasibility: 0≤w⋆​(y)≤M0\leq w^{\star}(y)\leq M and 𝔼y∼πref​[w⋆​(y)]=1\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w^{\star}(y)]=1.

(ii) Dual feasibility: μ⋆​(y)≥0\mu^{\star}(y)\geq 0 and ν⋆​(y)≥0\nu^{\star}(y)\geq 0 πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s.

(iii) Stationarity (pointwise): for πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s. yy,

s⁡(y)−α⋆+μ⋆​(y)−ν⋆​(y)=0.\displaystyle s(y)-\alpha^{\star}+\mu^{\star}(y)-\nu^{\star}(y)=0. (179)

(iv) Complementary slackness:

μ⋆(y)w⋆(y)=0,ν⋆(y)(M−w⋆(y))=0(πref-a.s.).\displaystyle\mu^{\star}(y)\,w^{\star}(y)=0,\qquad\nu^{\star}(y)\,(M-w^{\star}(y))=0\qquad(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\text{-a.s.}). (180)

We now deduce the threshold structure. Fix yy and consider three cases.

Case 1: 0<w⋆​(y)<M0<w^{\star}(y)<M. Then complementary slackness forces μ⋆​(y)=0\mu^{\star}(y)=0 and ν⋆​(y)=0\nu^{\star}(y)=0, and (179) gives s⁡(y)=α⋆s(y)=\alpha^{\star}.

Case 2: w⋆​(y)=0w^{\star}(y)=0. Then μ⋆​(y)≥0\mu^{\star}(y)\geq 0 may be nonzero, while ν⋆​(y)=0\nu^{\star}(y)=0 (since M−w⋆​(y)=M>0M-w^{\star}(y)=M>0 implies ν⋆​(y)=0\nu^{\star}(y)=0 by slackness). Thus (179) becomes s⁡(y)−α⋆+μ⋆​(y)=0s(y)-\alpha^{\star}+\mu^{\star}(y)=0, so s⁡(y)≤α⋆s(y)\leq\alpha^{\star}.

Case 3: w⋆​(y)=Mw^{\star}(y)=M. Then ν⋆​(y)≥0\nu^{\star}(y)\geq 0 may be nonzero, while μ⋆​(y)=0\mu^{\star}(y)=0 (since w⋆​(y)>0w^{\star}(y)>0 implies μ⋆​(y)=0\mu^{\star}(y)=0). Thus (179) becomes s⁡(y)−α⋆−ν⋆​(y)=0s(y)-\alpha^{\star}-\nu^{\star}(y)=0, so s⁡(y)≥α⋆s(y)\geq\alpha^{\star}.

Putting the three cases together yields the pointwise characterization:

w⋆​(y)={M,s⁡(y)>α⋆,0,s⁡(y)<α⋆,any value in ​[0,M],s⁡(y)=α⋆.\displaystyle w^{\star}(y)=\begin{cases}M,&s(y)>\alpha^{\star},\\ 0,&s(y)<\alpha^{\star},\\ \text{any value in }[0,M],&s(y)=\alpha^{\star}.\end{cases} (181)

Then the density ratio of the optimizer satisfies

w⋆(y)=M 1{s(y)≥α⋆}(πref-a.s.).\displaystyle w^{\star}(y)=M\,\mathbf{1}\{s(y)\geq\alpha^{\star}\}\qquad(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\text{-a.s.}). (182)

Finally, enforce the normalization 𝔼y∼πref​[w⋆​(y)]=1\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w^{\star}(y)]=1:

1=𝔼y∼πref​[w⋆​(y)]=M​ℙy∼πref​(s⁡(y)≥α⋆),\displaystyle 1=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}[w^{\star}(y)]=M\,\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big(s(y)\geq\alpha^{\star}\big), (183)

so ℙy∼πref​(s⁡(y)≥α⋆)=1/M\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(s(y)\geq\alpha^{\star})=1/M. Then the induced policy is precisely πM=πref(⋅∣s≥α∗)\pi_{M}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid s\geq\alpha^{*}). ∎

D.2 Proof of Theorem 5

Proof.

Fix M≥1M\geq 1 and let k:=⌈N/M⌉k:=\lceil N/M\rceil. Recall that π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} is the (unconditional) law of the random output youty_{\mathrm{out}} produced by: sample y1,…,yN​∼iid​πrefy_{1},\dots,y_{N}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and i.i.d. V1,…,VN∼Unif⁡[0,1]V_{1},\dots,V_{N}\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] independent; let II index the top-kk samples under the lexicographic order (r^​(yi),Vi)(\widehat{r}(y_{i}),V_{i}); output yJy_{J} with JJ uniform on II conditional on (𝒴^N,V1:N)(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N},V_{1:N}). To compare the performance of π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} to that of an arbitrary comparator π⋆\pi^{\star}, we proceed in a similar fashion to the proof of Theorem 3 in Section C.1 by considering the following regret decomposition:

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr⋆​(π^M)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}) =(Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆))⏟(T1)+(Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^M))⏟(T2)+(Rr^​(π^M)−Rr⋆​(π^M))⏟(T3).\displaystyle=\underbrace{\left(R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\right)}_{\mathrm{(T1)}}+\underbrace{\left(R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\right)}_{\mathrm{(T2)}}+\underbrace{\left(R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\right)}_{\mathrm{(T3)}}. (184)

As in the proof of Theorem 3, πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} is an intermediate comparator policy defined to be the policy that minimizes total variation distance to π⋆\pi^{\star} subject to the constraint that its density ratio relative to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is upper bounded by MM almost surely. To bound (T1)\mathrm{(T1)}, we can further decompose into

Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)=Rr⋆​(π⋆)−Rr^​(π⋆)+Rr^​(π⋆)−Rr^​(πM⋆)\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})=R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star})+R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M}) (185)

and control each of the two terms separately. For the first difference, we can simply invoke Lemma 4, which states that for any policy π\pi,

|Rr⋆(π)−Rr^(π)|≤Mεpw+ℰM(π∥πref).\displaystyle\big|R^{r^{\star}}(\pi)-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)\big|\;\leq\;M\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (186)

Applying this with π=π⋆\pi=\pi^{\star} yields

Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr^(π⋆)≤Mεpw+ℰM(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star})\leq M\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (187)

For the second difference, as in the proof of Theorem 3, we observe that win-rate is bounded and thus 11-Lipschitz in total variation distance (it can be written as an expectation of F~r^​(r^​(y))∈[0,1]\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))\in[0,1] by Lemma 5), so we can control the loss from π⋆\pi^{\star} to πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} in terms of ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) by Block and Polyanskiy [2]: Lemma 6 shows that no policy with bounded density ratio can achieve total variation distance to π⋆\pi^{\star} less than ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) itself, and Lemma 7 demonstrates that the total variation distance between π⋆\pi^{\star} and πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} as defined above is less than ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), so TV(π⋆,πM⋆)=ℰM(π⋆∥πref)\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star},\pi^{\star}_{M})=\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), and hence

Rr^(π⋆)−Rr^(πM⋆)≤TV(π⋆,πM⋆)=ℰM(π⋆∥πref).\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\leq\mathrm{TV}(\pi^{\star},\pi^{\star}_{M})=\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}). (188)

Putting these together, we have

(T1)=Rr⋆(π⋆)−Rr^(πM⋆)≲ℰM(π⋆∥πref)+Mεpw.\displaystyle\mathrm{(T1)}=R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\lesssim\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}. (189)

Next, to bound (T2)\mathrm{(T2)}, we again decompose further as

Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^M)=Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM)+Rr^​(πM)−Rr^​(π^M).\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})=R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})+R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}). (190)

Here, we introduce another intermediate comparator πM\pi_{M}, the solution to the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-regularized variational problem (10) and the “idealized” version of π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} which selects uniformly from a top-1/M1/M tail under r^\widehat{r}. To make this concrete, we derive the solution to (10) in Proposition 4 with s=r^s=\widehat{r}, writing the resulting threshold as λM\lambda_{M} so that ℙy∼πref​(s⁡(y)≥α⋆)=1/M\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(s(y)\geq\alpha^{\star})=1/M exactly. Thus, the optimizer has bounded density ratio of the form

wM⋆(y)=M 1{r^(y)≥λM},\displaystyle w_{M}^{\star}(y)\;=\;M\,\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda_{M}\}, (191)

πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-a.s. and λM\lambda_{M} is the (1−1M)(1-\tfrac{1}{M})-quantile of r^\widehat{r} under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, so the optimal policy is the top-1/M1/M threshold policy

πM(⋅)=πref(⋅∣r^(⋅)≥λM).\displaystyle\pi_{M}(\cdot)\;=\;\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\left(\cdot\mid\widehat{r}(\cdot)\geq\lambda_{M}\right). (192)

Now, for the first difference, recall that by Lemma 5 we can rewrite Rr^​(π)=𝔼y∼π​[F~r^​(r^​(y))]R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))]. Since F~r^​(⋅)\widetilde{F}_{\widehat{r}}(\cdot) is non-decreasing, πM\pi_{M} (output by Proposition 4 with s=r^s=\widehat{r}) maximizes Rr^​(π)R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi) over the class of policies with density ratio bounded by MM. Recalling that πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{M} is also subject to this constraint, it follows that Rr^​(πM⋆)≤Rr^​(πM)R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})\leq R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M}), and hence

Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(πM)≤0.\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})\leq 0. (193)

We now bound the second difference by directly comparing the win-rate of the ideal top-1/M1/M threshold policy πM\pi_{M} to that of our implementation π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M}. A convenient way to analyze Rr^​(π^M)R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}) when r^\widehat{r} may have ties is to “forget the scale” of r^\widehat{r} and work with a randomized quantile that induces a strict total order under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. Letting Fr^F_{\widehat{r}} and Fr^(⋅−)F_{\widehat{r}}(\cdot^{-}) be as in Lemma 5, and given an auxiliary seed V∼Unif⁡[0,1]V\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] independent of yy, we define

u~​(y,V):=Fr^​(r^​(y)−)+V⋅(Fr^​(r^​(y))−Fr^​(r^​(y)−))∈[0,1].\displaystyle\tilde{u}(y;V)\;:=\;F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\;+\;V\cdot\left(F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))-F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\right)\in[0,1]. (194)

Indeed, u~​(y,V)\tilde{u}(y;V) is exactly the randomized CDF value: it is strictly increasing in r^​(y)\widehat{r}(y), and on a tie r^​(y)=t\widehat{r}(y)=t it reduces to an independent linear interpolation over the CDF jump at tt, so ordering by (r^,V)(\widehat{r},V) is the same as ordering by u~\tilde{u}. Then for y′∼πrefy^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and V′∼Unif⁡[0,1]V^{\prime}\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] independent, Lemma 5 shows that u~​(y′,V′)∼Unif⁡[0,1]\tilde{u}(y^{\prime};V^{\prime})\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1], and moreover the win-rate under r^\widehat{r} can be realized as a strict comparison of these randomized quantiles: for any (possibly randomized) output yy,

ℙ⁡(r^​(y)>r^​(y′))+12​ℙ​(r^​(y)=r^​(y′))=ℙ⁡(u~​(y,V)>u~​(y′,V′)).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\right)\;+\;\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\right)\;=\;\mathbb{P}\left(\tilde{u}(y;V)>\tilde{u}(y^{\prime};V^{\prime})\right). (195)

(Indeed, if r^​(y)≠r^​(y′)\widehat{r}(y)\neq\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}) the inequality agrees with u~\tilde{u} by monotonicity, while if r^​(y)=r^​(y′)\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}) then u~​(y,V)>u~​(y′,V′)\tilde{u}(y;V)>\tilde{u}(y^{\prime};V^{\prime}) iff V>V′V>V^{\prime}, which occurs with probability 1/21/2.) Recalling that π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} uses uniform tie-breaking as described in the beginning of the proof, under (194), ranking by (r^​(yi),Vi)(\widehat{r}(y_{i}),V_{i}) is equivalent to ranking by u~i:=u~​(yi,Vi)\tilde{u}_{i}:=\tilde{u}(y_{i};V_{i}), and u~1,…,u~N​∼iid​Unif​[0,1]\tilde{u}_{1},\dots,\tilde{u}_{N}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}{\rm Unif}[0,1]. Thus, we compute Rr^​(π^M)R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}) via uniform order statistics in Lemma 11, which implies the lower bound

Rr^​(π^M)≥1−12​M−1N+1.\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\geq 1-\frac{1}{2M}-\frac{1}{N+1}. (196)

Next, we calculate the win-rate of the ideal top-1/M1/M quantile policy πM\pi_{M}. This should be intuitive, as under πM\pi_{M}, the draw y∼πMy\sim\pi_{M} lies in the r^\widehat{r}-upper tail of πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} of mass 1/M1/M, so against an independent y′∼πrefy^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} it wins whenever r^​(y)>r^​(y′)\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}) (which happens with probability 1−1/M1-1/M), and ties occur exactly when y′y^{\prime} also falls in the same tail (probability 1/M1/M), contributing a factor 12\tfrac{1}{2} under our win-rate convention. Lemma 10 formalizes this intuition and gives

Rr^​(πM)=1−12​M,\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})=1-\frac{1}{2M}, (197)

assuming feasibility of ℙπref​(r^≥λM)=1/M\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\widehat{r}\geq\lambda_{M})=1/M as we did in Proposition 4. Combining (196) and (197) yields

Rr^​(πM)−Rr^​(π^M)≲1N.\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\lesssim\frac{1}{N}. (198)

Thus, we have

(T2)=Rr^​(πM⋆)−Rr^​(π^M)≲1N.\displaystyle\mathrm{(T2)}=R^{\widehat{r}}(\pi^{\star}_{M})-R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\lesssim\frac{1}{N}. (199)

Finally, to bound (T3)\mathrm{(T3)}, we will first show that ℰM(π^M∥πref)=0\mathcal{E}_{M}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0 before applying Lemma 4 to π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M}. Let A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F} be measurable. Conditional on (𝒴^N,V1:N)(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N},V_{1:N}), the algorithm outputs yout=yJy_{\rm out}=y_{J} with J∼Unif(I(𝒴^N,V1:N))J\sim\mathrm{Unif}(I(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N},V_{1:N})), hence

π^M​(A)\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}_{M}(A) =𝔼𝒴^N∼πref,V1:N∼Unif[0,1]N[ℙ(yout∈A|𝒴^N,V1:N)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}},\;V_{1:N}\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1]^{N}}\!\left[\mathbb{P}\left(y_{\rm out}\in A\,\middle|\,\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N},V_{1:N}\right)\right] (200)
=𝔼𝒴^N,V1:N[1k∑i∈I(𝒴^N,V1:N)𝟏{yi∈A}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N},V_{1:N}}\!\left[\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in I(\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N},V_{1:N})}\mathbf{1}\{y_{i}\in A\}\right] (201)
≤𝔼𝒴^N,V1:N[1k∑i=1N𝟏{yi∈A}]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{N},V_{1:N}}\!\left[\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{y_{i}\in A\}\right] (202)

wπ^M​(y):=d​π^Md​πref​(y)≤Nkπref​-a.s.\displaystyle w_{\widehat{\pi}_{M}}(y):=\frac{d\widehat{\pi}_{M}}{d\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(y)\leq\frac{N}{k}\quad\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\text{-a.s.} (204)

Lemma 10.

Let λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} and Aλ:={y:r^​(y)≥λ}A_{\lambda}:=\{y:\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda\} with pλ:=ℙy∼πref​(Aλ)p_{\lambda}:=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(A_{\lambda}). Let π~λ:=πref(⋅∣Aλ)\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda}:=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid A_{\lambda}). Then

Rr^​(π~λ)=1−pλ2.\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda})=1-\frac{p_{\lambda}}{2}. (208)
Proof.

Fix λ\lambda and let Aλ={y:r^​(y)≥λ}A_{\lambda}=\{y:\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda\}, pλ=πref​(Aλ)p_{\lambda}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(A_{\lambda}), and π~λ=πref(⋅∣Aλ)\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid A_{\lambda}). Then, for π~λ\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda}, r^​(y)≥λ\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda always. To compute the win-rate of π~λ\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda}, we can split on the event that r^​(y′)≥λ\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda:

Rr^​(π~λ)\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda}) =ℙy∼π~λ,y′∼πref​(r^​(y)>r^​(y′))+12​ℙy∼π~λ,y′∼πref​(r^​(y)=r^​(y′))\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda},y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\right)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda},y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\right) (209)
=ℙ⁡(r^​(y′)<λ)+ℙ⁡(r^​(y)>r^​(y′),r^​(y′)≥λ)+12​ℙ​(r^​(y)=r^​(y′),r^​(y′)≥λ)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})<\lambda\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}),\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}),\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right) (210)
=(1−pλ)+ℙ⁡(r^​(y)>r^​(y′),r^​(y′)≥λ)+12​ℙ​(r^​(y)=r^​(y′),r^​(y′)≥λ).\displaystyle=(1-p_{\lambda})+\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}),\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}),\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right). (211)

Next, we condition on the event {r^​(y)≥λ,r^​(y′)≥λ}\{\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda,\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\}, which is implied by the events in the last two terms in the equation above. Let

q:=ℙ⁡(r^​(y)>r^​(y′)|r^​(y)≥λ,r^​(y′)≥λ),t:=ℙ⁡(r^​(y)=r^​(y′)|r^​(y)≥λ,r^​(y′)≥λ).\displaystyle q\;:=\;\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\,\big|\,\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda,\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right),\qquad t\;:=\;\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\,\big|\,\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda,\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right). (212)

By exchangeability, the events {r^(y)>r^(y′)}\{\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\} and {r^(y′)>r^(y)}\{\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})>\widehat{r}(y)\} have the same conditional probability, and together with ties they partition the conditional sample space, hence 2​q+t=12q+t=1, implying q+12​t=12q+\frac{1}{2}t=\frac{1}{2}. Therefore, by Bayes’ Theorem,

ℙ⁡(r^​(y)>r^​(y′),r^​(y′)≥λ)+12​ℙ​(r^​(y)=r^​(y′),r^​(y′)≥λ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}),\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime}),\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right) =ℙ⁡(r^​(y)≥λ,r^​(y′)≥λ)⋅(q+12​t)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda,\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right)\cdot\left(q+\frac{1}{2}t\right) (213)
=12​ℙ​(r^​(y)≥λ,r^​(y′)≥λ).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda,\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right). (214)

Finally, note that

ℙ⁡(r^​(y)≥λ,r^​(y′)≥λ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y)\geq\lambda,\ \widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\geq\lambda\right) =ℙy∼π~λ,y′∼πref​(y∈Aλ,y′∈Aλ)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda},y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(y\in A_{\lambda},\ y^{\prime}\in A_{\lambda}\right) (215)
=1pλ​ℙy∼πref,y′∼πref​(y∈Aλ,y′∈Aλ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{\lambda}}\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}},y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(y\in A_{\lambda},\ y^{\prime}\in A_{\lambda}\right) (216)
=pλ.\displaystyle=p_{\lambda}. (217)

Plugging in gives

Rr^​(π~λ)=1−pλ2.\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda})=1-\frac{p_{\lambda}}{2}. (218)

Lemma 11.

Fix M≥1M\geq 1 and integer N≥1N\geq 1, and let k:=⌈N/M⌉k:=\lceil N/M\rceil. Then the win-rate of π^M\widehat{\pi}_{M} against πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} under r^\widehat{r} is

Rr^​(π^M)= 1−k+12​(N+1).\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\;=\;1-\frac{k+1}{2(N+1)}. (219)
Proof.

Let Fr^F_{\widehat{r}} and Fr^(⋅−)F_{\widehat{r}}(\cdot^{-}) be as in Lemma 5, and define the randomized quantile

u~​(y,V):=Fr^​(r^​(y)−)+V⁡(Fr^​(r^​(y))−Fr^​(r^​(y)−)).\displaystyle\tilde{u}(y;V)\;:=\;F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})+V\left(F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y))-F_{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{r}(y)^{-})\right). (220)

Set u~i:=u~​(yi,Vi)\tilde{u}_{i}:=\tilde{u}(y_{i};V_{i}). The randomized-PIT argument provided in Lemma 5 gives

u~1,…,u~N​∼iid​Unif​[0,1].\displaystyle\tilde{u}_{1},\dots,\tilde{u}_{N}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}{\rm Unif}[0,1]. (221)

Moreover, by construction, ordering the indices by (r^​(yi),Vi)(\widehat{r}(y_{i}),V_{i}) is equivalent to ordering them by u~i\tilde{u}_{i} (since ties in r^\widehat{r} are broken by ViV_{i}, which exactly corresponds to the interpolation inside each CDF jump).

Let youty_{\rm out} denote the algorithm output and define u~out:=u~​(yout,VJ)\tilde{u}_{\rm out}:=\tilde{u}(y_{\rm out};V_{J}). Introduce an independent “opponent” draw y′∼πrefy^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and V′∼Unif⁡[0,1]V^{\prime}\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] independent of everything, and write u~′:=u~​(y′,V′)∼Unif⁡[0,1]\tilde{u}^{\prime}:=\tilde{u}(y^{\prime};V^{\prime})\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1]. Then

Rr^​(π^M)\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M}) =ℙ⁡(r^​(yout)>r^​(y′))+12​ℙ​(r^​(yout)=r^​(y′))\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y_{\rm out})>\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\right)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{r}(y_{\rm out})=\widehat{r}(y^{\prime})\right) (222)
=ℙ⁡(u~out>u~′)=𝔼⁡[u~out],\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\tilde{u}_{\rm out}>\tilde{u}^{\prime}\right)=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{u}_{\rm out}], (223)

where the last step uses u~′∼Unif⁡[0,1]\tilde{u}^{\prime}\sim{\rm Unif}[0,1] independent of u~out\tilde{u}_{\rm out}.

Now condition on the realized batch (u~1,…,u~N)(\tilde{u}_{1},\dots,\tilde{u}_{N}) and u~(1)≤⋯≤u~(N)\tilde{u}_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq\tilde{u}_{(N)} be the order statistics. Since JJ is uniform over the top-kk indices (under the u~\tilde{u}-ranking),

𝔼[u~out∣u~1,…,u~N]=1k∑j=N−k+1Nu~(j).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\big[\tilde{u}_{\rm out}\mid\tilde{u}_{1},\dots,\tilde{u}_{N}\big]=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=N-k+1}^{N}\tilde{u}_{(j)}. (224)

Taking expectations and using 𝔼⁡[u~(j)]=jN+1\mathbb{E}[\tilde{u}_{(j)}]=\frac{j}{N+1} for Unif⁡[0,1]{\rm Unif}[0,1] order statistics gives

Rr^​(π^M)=𝔼⁡[u~out]=1k​∑j=N−k+1N𝔼⁡[u~(j)]=1k​∑j=N−k+1NjN+1=1−k+12​(N+1).\displaystyle R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{u}_{\rm out}]=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=N-k+1}^{N}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{u}_{(j)}]=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=N-k+1}^{N}\frac{j}{N+1}=1-\frac{k+1}{2(N+1)}. (225)

Since |kN+1−1M|≤2N+1\big|\frac{k}{N+1}-\frac{1}{M}\big|\leq\frac{2}{N+1}, when k=⌈N/M⌉k=\lceil N/M\rceil, we in fact have

1−12​M−1N+1≤Rr^​(π^M)≤ 1−12​M+1N+1.\displaystyle 1-\frac{1}{2M}-\frac{1}{N+1}\;\leq\;R^{\widehat{r}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\;\leq\;1-\frac{1}{2M}+\frac{1}{N+1}. (226)
